How I saved $4,200 on 3 weeks in Portugal (without camping out) 
 This past January when I bought my trip to Portugal, my trip would have cost me $6,800 if I had to pay full price. But I ended up paying about $2,600 for it. Here's the breakdown. 
 Flight: $1,850 in savings 
 I had 68K Chase Sapphire preferred points and some work United miles from the last 2 years. In mid September, I got a transfer bonus. 25% bonus points when transferring to United from Chase. So this gave me enough points to use to get a round trip saver ticket from Newark to Lisbon. $121 in taxes and fees, saving $982 from the $982 price it would have been in Feb when I would have travelled. 
 I timed it right, flew from Jan 9-30. Post holiday mid winter flights to Europe from the Northeast fall off a cliff. Would have cost over $1,400 for the same trip in June. 
 Accommodation: $1,600 in savings 
 I spent 3 weeks there (8N in Lisbon, 6N in Porto, 7N in Lagos in the Algarve) I did not stay in hotels. Booked apartments on booking.com in January - prime off season time when owners are grasping at any straws for bookings. $54/night for a 1 bed apartment in Alfama in Lisbon for example. What would that have been in June? $150 or so probably. 
 Guesthouse with ocean view room in Lagos for $47/night with breakfast. Plus I used a credit card portal so through the chase portal with my sapphire card, I essentially got another 5% in points for booking on the chase portal. 
 Other: $750+ in savings 
 Museum: Lisbon card. 72h for 42€. Allowed me to enter Jeronimos Monastery and Belém tower. Access to public transport as well. Saved me about 60€ 
 Off-season tours: Did the Douro Valley wine tour out of Porto. Saved 55€ (instead of 85€ which it would have been in summer). Less people too. Only 6 of us, instead of a van full. 
 Eating: Jan meant I didn't need reservations to Taberna da Rua das Flores in Lisbon. Just walked in on a Tuesday. Eating the same dinner. No tourist markups. 
 Trade offs (honesty) 
 Rain for 4 days in Porto. Some restaurants at beach in Lagos closed. Short days (sunset around 5:30pm) But it was still 60F in Lisbon most days in the afternoon in Jan. Pena palace in Sintra. Basically all to myself one Wednesday morning. In summer, it's 2hr line. 
 So the savings: 
 Flight $1,850 
 Accommodation $1,600 
 Tours/attractions $750 
 Total $4,200. Fund my next trip (already thinking about it) 
 Greece in November anyone?

blog_personal_02_sonnet.text:
I think my garage will always smell like PB Blaster now.
I bought it August 2nd. 
A dude named Russ in Hillsboro has had it sitting under a tarp since 2011. 
It's a 78 Honda CB750K. 
31400 miles. 
Matte with dust. 
$1400 cash. 
Odometer cable siezed. 
Carbs varnished to death. 
A family of something was living in the airbox. 
Duh. It's the original owner of the bike in ten years. 
 
Degrease it for the first week. 
4 cans of simple green and one Saturday. 
Blew all the shit off of the engine cases that had accumulated there in 11 years. 
Finally able to see what I was working with. 
Cases are actually in really nice condition. 
No cracks. 
No stripped threads. 
Just cosmetic corrosion on the fin edge. 
 
Second week. 
Ripped the carb bank out of there. 
(4 Keihin CV carburetors) 
Let them soak in a Berryman's dip for 3 days. 
Rebuilt them using a kit from CB750Supply. 
$89 for all 4 sets of gaskets and O-rings and float valves. 
Man, that was the best afternoon of working on this thing so far. 
Watching crusted float bowls open up clean. 
 
So far (keeping track in notebook on workbench)
Bought the bike. $1400
Rebuild kit for the carbs $89
Battery (YB9-B cause the battery was a brick) $34
New fuel lines and inline filter $22
Degreaser. Brushes. Gloves. Shop rags. ~$60
Spark plugs NGK 4 pack $18
 
So far. As of tonight 9.20.19 $1623
 
Compression is 145-148-142-140 psi across the four cylinders. 
Man. Feels like winning the lottery on a 48 year old air cooled engine. 
Haven't tried to start it yet. 
Trying to next weekend. 
Get fresh gas in there. 
Gap the points. 
Neighbor Dave (rebuilt 2 of these) says don't rush that first kick. 
Yea. I'm gonna rush it.

blog_personal_04_luna.text:
January 8, 2025. Running shoes on my feet. Age 51. Goal: complete my first half marathon post knee replacement. 

Not a year ago, this seemed laughable. I had my right knee replaced in March 2024. Years of arthritis had made it challenging to walk up stairs, take long walks and even getting out of the car a real pain. The recovery period was long and humbling. Physical Therapist, Elena Morales, had me taking 5 min walks around my Sacramento, CA neighborhood. By June I could walk two miles non-stop. By September I was cycling (stationary bike) and performing strength exercises three days a week. 

But there was no way I could run! Until my friend Marcus mentioned the Davis Turkey Trot Half Marathon. Date? November 27, 2025. "You don't need to run all the time." He explained. "Just need to train."

So I tried a walk-run program. 1 min jog/ 2 min walk. Repeat for 20 min. Total distance for my first workout? 1.4 miles. Knee was swollen. Iced it. Called Elena. Learned a critical lesson: progress and pain don't always go hand in hand. 

Today. I train four times a week. Easy walk runs on Tuesdays. Strength exercises on Thursdays. Longer - slower runs on Saturdays. Sunday I stretch and recover. I only add up to 1/2 mile to my long distance each week. Three miles in February. Six miles in April. Last Saturday I ran 9 miles. Along the American River Parkway. Two hours and 11 minutes. 

I'm not aiming for PR. I just want to finish the Davis half marathon course before it's closed. Ideally with a smile on my face. Still be able to walk. I'm aware that my speed will not be what it was when I was 30. Mostly because I didn't run back when I was 30. But the miles I run are a constant reminder of what my body is still capable of. 

I am 51. Titanium knee. Highly patient training regime. Realizing that sometimes starting over is a win.

January 8th, 2025. 51 years old. Shoe tying. Lacing up the running shoes. One thing in mind: complete my first half marathon following knee replacement.

It would have seemed insane a year ago. I had knee replacement on my right knee in March 2024. Years of arthritis caused the stairs, long walks, and even getting in and out of the car to be excruciating. It was a challenging and humbling journey. I began walking in my neighborhood in Sacramento, CA with PT, Elena Morales. She had me starting with five minute walks. June, I could walk 2 miles straight. September, I added 3x/week stationary bike and strength.

But running? Nah. That's not an option. Until my friend Marcus mentioned the Davis Turkey Trot Half Marathon. November 27th, 2025. 'You don't have to run it. Just have to train hard.'

So I start with a walk/run plan. 1 minute of jogging and then 2 minutes of walking. For 20 minutes. 1.4 miles on my first workout. Swollen knee at the end. Ice the knee. Phone call to Elena. Lesson: More progress doesn't mean more pain.

I'm at 4x a week now. Tuesday is easy walk/run. Thursday is strength. Saturday is longer, slower. Sunday is stretching/recovery. I only add 1/2 mile or less each week for longer distance. 3 miles in February. 6 miles in April. Last Saturday, I ran 9 miles on the American River Parkway. 2h11m.

Not going after a PR. I just want to make it to the finish line in Davis. Before they close the course. And if possible, I'd like to do it with a smile on my face and still be able to walk after. I know my pace is going to be much slower than it was at 30. Mostly because I wasn't running when I was 30. But it's a reminder of my body's potential. A reminder each mile that it can still surprise me.

Titanium knee. 51 years old. Very patient training plan. I'm realizing that starting over can be its own kind of win.

blog_personal_06_glm.text:
Co-Parenting a Long Distance and Across Time Zones: Navigating School Events from Berlin to Toronto

In September 2023, Marcus accepted a teaching job in Berlin. This created some interesting co-parenting situations. I remained in Toronto with our two children (Elena 11 and Theo 8). While six time zones might not seem that long a distance, when you need to navigate parent teacher nights it can be a challenge.

This is what we've learned 18 months into the new arrangement.

Shared calendars are everything. One Google calendar. School events. Swim lessons at Wallace Emerson Community Centre. Theo's Wednesday speech therapy at 4pm (Toronto). If it's not on there, it doesn't happen. Marcus checks it as part of his morning routine at 7am (Berlin), which is 1am for me, so he can see anything I've planned for the night before and it hasn't yet registered with me.

Shift who attends. Marcus can't be in the gymnasium at Earl Grey Public School physically, but he makes sure he participates in parent teacher interviews (via video). Generally he's on at 8pm or 9pm (his time). The teachers have been great about accommodating early interviews for Elena. For events where we need to be physically present (winter concert, march break pickup) he buys flights. He's visited four times so far staying in a rental near our home in Dovercourt Road.

The kids and Marcus have "Berlin dinner" on Tuesday and Friday. 2:30pm for Marcus. He has lunch while the kids have dinner and chats with them about their week. Theo likes showing off his Lego creations through the camera. Elena mainly just eye rolls but she doesn't miss it. We really protect those times. No play dates can be scheduled for those times.

There are definitely struggles. Marcus felt helpless when Theo had the flu in February (2023) and I had to stay up all night with him. He was 6600km away. We've learned that there's still ways he can be helpful. Marcus does all the digital stuff from overseas. Orders school supplies, schedules Theo's therapy appointments, searches for march break camps. Practical help is still helpful.

The kids have some strange skills. Time zone conversion. Theo can do Toronto to Berlin faster than I can. We have that time difference thing going on with daylight savings. Sometimes it changes at different times for North America and Europe (for example Europe changes 2 weeks earlier than North America in the spring). This means we have to deal with a 5 hour difference for 2 weeks. Everyone is confused.

Our situation is not what we anticipated when we split up in 2021. Elena recently shared with her counselor at school. She has "a dad in two countries." She made it sound like it was a super power.

If you're in a similar situation. 1) shared calendar. 2) protected call times. 3) divide invisible labour across continents. It's not perfect but it works for us.

LONG DISTANCE CO-PARENTING THROUGH TIME ZONES: HOW TO CO-NAVIGATE SCHOOL FROM BERLIN & TORONTO

In Sept 2023, when Marcus landed the teaching job at Humboldt University, we knew it would be a co-parenting challenge. He was off to Berlin and we’d be in Toronto with our two children, Elena (11) and Theo (8). Cool, 6 hours time difference. Until you need to get to a parent-teacher evening.

This is what we’ve learned in our 18 months of time-zone co-parenting.

1) EVERYTHING GOES IN THE CALENDAR. NO EXCEPTIONS. The one Google Calendar. Swim at Wallace Emerson Community Centre. Parent-teacher night. 4 pm Wed Speech therapy for Theo in Toronto. If it’s not in the calendar, it doesn’t exist. And Marcus looks at it with his coffee at 7am (1am for me) Berlin time. So, he sees anything from my night, before I’m awake.

2) SWITCHED PARENT PRESENCE. Even though Marcus can’t literally be in the gym at Earl Grey Public School, he can (and does) do video-parent-teacher meetings (often at 8/9pm his time). Elena’s teachers are great about setting earlier times. When Marcus really needs to be there in the flesh (winter concert, March Break pick-up), he flies in. He’s been here 4 times now. We have a rental near us on Dovercourt Rd.

3) Berlin dinner T/F for the kids. That’s 2:30pm for Marcus, so he eats lunch and they eat dinner. They chat about the week. Theo likes to show Marcus LEGO creations through the camera. Elena mostly eye-rolls, but never misses. This is sacred time. No play dates during this time.

4) It’s tough. Like when Theo got the flu last Feb, and I’m up all night. And Marcus is 6,600 kms away feeling helpless. We’ve learned that he CAN help. He does all online tasks (ordering school supplies, booking Theo’s therapy appointments, looking into March Break camps) from abroad. Practical help IS help.

5) Time Zone math is a bizarre new skill for the kids. And Theo can calculate from Toronto to Berlin faster than me. And when we change daylight savings at different times (Europe 2 weeks ahead in the Spring before North America) we go through 2 weeks of 5 hour time difference. And it confuses everyone.

6) It’s not the ideal set-up we thought up when we separated in 2021. But the other day, when Elena told her school counselor she “has a dad in two countries.” It sounded like a superpower to her. Sure.

7) So, if you are doing the time zone co-parenting thing - shared calendar. Protected phone times. Divide up the invisible labor by continent. Imperfect, but it’s our way.

I finished a shift at St. Lukes Medical Center on a Tuesday in July 2024. Started a UX bootcamp the following Monday. Just finished 3 weeks in the role of product designer at a healthtech startup in Providence.

Let me document exactly what went down, because what I thought the timeline would be has 0% resemblance to the timeline that actually was.

Month 1-3: The part time UX/UI class at General Assembly. Three 12 hour night shifts a week at the hospital. 7am I finished my shift. 1pm I wake up. 3pm I start the cohort call. (for the 3pm cohort). Completed two projects. Redesign the patient discharge instructions at my hospital (the patient discharge instructions at my hospital were fucking abysmal, trust me, now that I look at it as a designer rather than just a nurse giving them out.) And Dosewise, a medication reminder app.

Month 4-7: THE IN BETWEEN. In November 2024 I full stop quit nursing. (We saved 8 months worth of expenses for exactly this purpose.) Months 4-7 were informational interviews. 34 informational interviews. I kept them in a spreadsheet. I found them mostly through a UX meetup in Providence: Ocean State UX. Second Thursday of every month in a coworking space on Westminster street. 11 of the calls were to give portfolio feedback.

Month 8-10: Third case study, and this one was unsolicited. Redesign the nurse shift handoff tool at my former hospital. I did interviews with 6 previous colleagues about where the info was lost from shift to shift. This was my project with the most callbacks by far. Because this is the one where I used my background as a nurse to its full advantage, rather than having to explain my background.

Month 11-14: 61 apps, 9 first interviews, 3 final interviews. 1 offer.
Offer came from a healthtech startup called Verve Health. 40 people. Building tools for home health aides. Sept 2, 2025.
$89,000 starting. Was $6,000 less than what I made last year as a nurse with differentials. But no more nights!

If you're beginning now, prepare yourself for nothingness in month 5-7. It's not nothingness, it's interviews compounding.

blog_personal_10_luna.text:
Eli was 8 when we started homeschooling him in September of 2022. Reading at about a 1st grade level. He was dyslexic. So every worksheet was a test that he already failed. He could draw you a fancy picture about the water cycle and understand it. But read a short paragraph on it and he would be so tired and so embarrassed. 
 In the first year we tried 3 of the popular language arts programs. One focused too much on reading on their own. Another was flying through spelling words too fast. Neither program made it longer than 6 weeks. All about reading level 2 and all about spelling got us there. Short 20 minute lessons. Very explicit about phonograms. Syllables. Blending. Letter tiles. Table tapping of the sounds. Decoding books. Not picture guessing. February of 2023 we got to a point where he could read simple chapter books out loud. And not shut down. 
 Writing. Institute of excellence in writing, primary arts of language. Loved it because it kept the writing and coming up with ideas separate. Initially I had him dictate what he was writing to me. And I typed it out. Then he would copy sentences. Then two sentences. And finally writing paragraphs. He had a blast writing a version of "The Three Little Pigs" from the wolf's perspective. 
 Math wasn't as bad. But word problems were a challenge because of the reading making it hard to demonstrate. Math U see was great. Hands on. Predictable. And we spent close to two months on multiplication with colorful blocks. Then we moved to written multiplication problems. I would read every single word problem. And he could draw the problem or verbally explain his thought. 
 So we just slowed down. About 3 hours of intense learning each morning. Movement breaks every 25 minutes. Not trying to keep up with the local school schedule. Eli read an entire 120 page adventure book in May of 2024. On his own. Took him almost 3 weeks. But he did it! And wanted to read the next book in the series right away. 
 The dyslexia didn't go away. And homeschooling didn't become easy. But the right curriculum made it where he was given tools instead of feeling pressure. Most importantly, he learned he is capable.

We homeschooled Eli starting Sept 2022. He was 8 years old reading like a first grader. He had dyslexia and every worksheet was like he was failing a test. He could draw the water cycle for you in great detail. If you gave him a small paragraph to read about the water cycle, he was mentally fatigued and feeling stupid. 
 Over the course of 12 months, we tried several (well known) language arts programs. One was too much independent reading. One went through spelling lists too quickly. Most programs lasted 6 weeks at most. All About reading level 2 and All About spelling were the programs that clicked for us. Short lessons of 20 mins or so. Ultra explicit with phonograms, syllables, blending. Letter tiles. Tapping out words on the table. Reading decodable books instead of relying on pictures. By Feb 2023, Eli was able to read simple chapter books out loud without mental meltdowns. 
 For writing, we did Institute for excellence in writing, primary arts of language. I liked that it allowed writing the physical stuff and the creative thought stuff to be separate. Initially he dictated his answers to me and I typed them. Slowly he started copying one sentence, then 2 sentences, then finally short paragraphs. One of his favorite things was changing "The 3 little pigs" to the wolf's perspective. 
 Math was a little less painful but reading was an issue for word problems because it was blocking him from demonstrating his knowledge. Math U see was great. It was hands on and consistent. We did multiplication for close to 2 months with blocks. Color blocks. Then started into writing equations. I read out loud for every word problem. He could either draw the word problem or verbalize his thoughts. 
 Most of all, it was slowing down. We school about 3 intense hours in the morning. Movement breaks every 25 mins or so. And quit trying to match up with what the local school does. By may 2024, Eli was able to read a whole 120 page adventure book on his own. It took nearly 3 weeks, but he finished it. Then he wanted to read the next book in the series. 
 It doesn't mean the dyslexia is gone and homeschooling is a walk in the park. However, finding the right curricula gave Eli some tools and not as much pressure. More importantly, it helped him feel like he can do this.

blog_personal_12_glm.text:
Mom is 65 and asked for an upgrade to her bday party last june: 11 days of Tour du Mont Blanc walking with her. No entire 170km TMB, made very clear from day one. The usual french and italian routes. We left out a few stages, bus riding and averaged 12km a day. (instead of 20+). 
 Best idea ever. 
 TMB online world is full of people pushing ultra light. Get up at 5am. Skip them for most part. 
 What worked: 
 - Packing.
 Mom pack was 7kg. Mine 10kg (incl shared first aid & wine purchases in courmayeur)
 Mom: 1x 40l pack. 2 x merino hiking shirts. 1x convertibles pants. Rain. Down jacket. +imperative=personal trekking poles.
 Mom had a knee replaced in 2021. She swore that trekking poles had made her legs 5 yrs younger. 
 I had too many shirts. I returned half in chamonix. 
 - Pace.
 We did 1 big climb per day and stop there. Nearly died day 3 climbing out of Les Contamines to Col du Bonhomme. (2329m)
 Rest of the trip structure:
 Start by 8:30ish
 Lunch in refuge around 12ish. (Tartiflette orders a must!)
 Stop walking by 3:30 for mom to have an hour of stretching/shower time before aperitif. 
 July is really booked for some refuges (Nant Borrant. Bonatti, rifugio). Book by March. 
 - Truth.
 She had tears at Fenetre Arpette lookout. (I did too). 
 Also. 2 days she took bus and I walked. (Les chapieux to courmayeur was fine. No regrets. She had espressos in the town. While I strained Col de la Seigne in the rain). 
 Truth: Pacing ain't bad.
 It's what made this trip possible. 
 If you're thinking of doing this with an old parent, make sure you book the flexible version of everything!
 Bring deck of cards. Refuge nights are long. She beat my ass at gin rummy every night. 
 Would I do it again?
 Walker's haute route is penciled for 70.
 She'll "train" this time.
 She won't.
 It'll be fine.

Last June my mom turned 65 and instead of a party, she wanted to do something better. She wanted 11 days of walking the Tour du Mont Blanc with me. And no, not the 170 km. We talked about it and she made it very clear from the get go that she didn't want all 170 km. We would walk the famous French & Italian routes. We'd skip a few stages where we'd ride buses. And we'd walk on average 12 km/day instead of the normal 20+ km. This was the best idea we had. 
 The TMB community is full of UL mavens and 5 am people. Mostly you should ignore these folks. Here's what actually worked for us: 
 1. Packing. 
 - Mom carried 7 kg. I carried 10 kg (this included the first aid supplies we both used and the wine we kept drinking in Courmayeur). 
 - Mom: 1 backpack 40L, 2 hiking merino shirts, 1 pair of convertible pants, rain shell, down jacket. She insisted on carrying her own trekking poles. She'd had a knee replacement in 2021 and she said it gave her 5 more years on her legs. 
 - I overpacked with too many shirts. Half went home from Chamonix. 
 2. Walk/Pace 
 - 1 big hike a day and then stop. 
 - Almost killed us on day 3 trying to get up from Les Contamines to Col du Bonhomme (2329m). We changed the game plan after this. 
 - Leave early, around 8:30. Eat lunch at a refuge around noon. (Order the Tartiflette!!!) Finish walking by 3:30. This gives mom 1 hr to stretch and shower before aperitif. 
 - Make reservations for some of the refuges months in advance (July). Places like Refuge Nant Borrant & Rifugio Bonatti need to be booked by March. 
 3. The truthful stuff 
 - She cried at the viewpoint at Fenêtre d'Arpette. I cried too. 
 - There were a couple of days she hopped the bus while I walked (Les Chapieux to Courmayeur). We don't regret it. She got to drink espresso in the town while I suffered in the rain crossing Col de la Seigne. 
 - Pace yourself and it's not about defeat. It's about making it all possible. 
 If you're planning on doing this with an older parent, book everything in the flexible way. And don't forget a deck of cards for those long nights at the refuge. Mom kicked my ass every night at gin rummy. 
 Would I do it again? Yes! We're already planning to do the Walker's Haute Route for her 70th birthday. She says she's going to train. But she won't. It'll be fine.

blog_personal_14_sonnet.text:
Two days after my 38th birthday, I impulsively enrolled in Clayworks on Fulton Street for the 6-week beginner wheel throwing class on a whim. My husband got it for me, as a joke, for my birthday. I never imagined I'd be doing this 14 months later. 
 My first bowl that I got centered took me 40 minutes. It ended up looking like a beret. My teacher, Marcus, was a sweet guy who had been throwing for 20 years. He's quiet. He said centering is 90% of the battle and you'll never get it in week 1. He was being generous. I didn't really get it till week 9. 
 For the first 4 months, everything I did was tilted. I have a mug from October. It's so tilted it looks like it's being poured all the time. I kept it on my desk. To remind me. I didn't toss it. My wife started calling early work of mine, "The Leaning Tower of Ceramics" 
 Then, in February, it happened. It was a Tuesday night class. I threw a set of four cereal bowls that match. Same height. Same thickness of wall. I could see light through the greenware, how thin the walls were. Marcus picked one up. He said, "OK, you're not battling the clay now." I went home and teared up. It's a bowl. 
 By June I had a glaze I liked. It's a break-y kind. Iron speckled, white. It's Shino. It does different things every firing. It depends on where it is in the kiln. I had 40 pieces piled up on the shelf. 
 My 10 year old daughter said, "Why don't you try the farmers market at Wallingford on Saturdays. The one near our house." $35 for a half table for one morning in August. 
 
 I sold 11 pieces. 3 mugs, 4 little bowls, a butter dish, 3 of those speckled cereal bowls I'm most proud of. All to one woman who says she's replacing everything. I made $187 off of it. But I've spent probably 4x that on class fees this year. It's not a business. But I had an empty box in my trunk when I got home. Not a full one. That was something. 
 I'm starting an intermediate class in October. Marcus says it's time for me to start learning how to trim right. I've got my beret bowl. Now I put my keys in it.

I did the whim 6 week beginner wheel course at Clayworks on Fulton street 2 days after my 38th bday. It was a stupid joke birthday gift that my husband got me. I never thought I'd still be there 14 months later.

My first bowl I centered took 40 min and was the shape of a beret. My teacher Marcus (a quiet guy who's been doing throwing for 20 years) said centering is 90% the battle and no one does it in week 1. He was a nice guy. I didn't get it until week 9.

For the first 4 months everything I made slants. I have this mug I made in Oct that slants so much it looks like it's pouring even when standing still. I kept it on my desk as a reminder instead of throwing it away. My wife started calling my early work "Leaning Tower of Ceramics".

In Feb. one Tuesday night class I made a set of 4 cereal bowls that were all the same. Same height. Same wall thickness. The wall thickness was thin enough to see light in the greenware. Marcus picked up one and says "now you're not fighting the clay". I got home and kinda teared up. For a bowl? 

June comes. I found a glaze I like. Breaky iron speckled white. It's called Shino. Can do different things each firing depending on the spot in the kiln. Got 40 things on a shelf with no home. My 10 year old daughter says do the farmers market Sat. at Wallingford. The one by our house. I pay $35 for 1/2 table for 1 morning in Aug.

I sell 11 pieces. 3 mugs. 4 small bowls. A butter dish. 3 of those awesome speckled cereal bowls. All to this lady who says she's replacing all her stuff. I make $187. I spent probably 4 times that in class fees this year. Not a business. But I got home with an empty box in the trunk. Not a full one. Feels good.

I'm in the intermediate class starting in Oct. Marcus says it's time I learn to trim correctly. I still have the beret bowl. It holds my keys now.

This is a quick email to ask for clarification on the interpretation of the Q3 regression of my economics term paper on the impact of minimum wage changes on part-time employment in California (2012-2023).

So my regression model shows that 10% increase in real minimum wage leads to a 0.8% decrease in part-time employment (coef = -0.080, p = 0.03) while controlling for county fixed effects, year fixed effects, unemployment, and industry composition.
 But I quote a Freakley (2021) study which finds no significant reduction in employment post minimum wage increase. So currently I write in my paper that this is "consistent with a small negative effect on employment". But is this not inconsistent with the study I cited? 
 
 Is it more appropriate to acknowledge it as a contradiction or to say something along the lines of "this is because the data and methodology differ"? Freakley study is using national quarterly data from 1990-2018 while I am using annual county level data for California (2012-2023) and concentrating on part-time workers. Also coefficient is no longer significant if I drop 2020-2021 so it seems that there is some impact from pandemic related disruption in labor market.
 
 Would you advise to rephrase the discussion to highlight these limitations in order not to say that there is some direct contradiction with Freakley?

 Jordan Lee

essay_opinion_01_luna.text:
Times Square should be car-free by 2030. And we should do it not as stunt but as a reasonable progression of New York's ongoing social experiment in returning public space to the public.

Times Square has been changing. In 2009, under Mayor Michael Bloomberg, Broadway was cut through Times Square and temporary pedestrian plazas began to pop up between 42nd and 47th Street. At the time it seemed bold, but soon it seemed normal. Fewer vehicle conflicts. More space for pedestrians. Tables, performances, standing. Standing still in one of the busiest parts of the world.

And yet, Times Square is still an oxymoron of a place. It is designed to overload the senses. Millions of people visit it annually. And yet, there are still cars and trucks slicing through all the activity. Every day over 300,000 pedestrians move through the space. They weave their way through barriers, delivery trucks, taxis, buses, turning vehicles. All while gazing up to the advertisements for New York as a place of potential.

A permanent car-free Times Square won't mean no vehicles. Access for emergency personnel, maintenance, accessibility, and scheduled deliveries could still be allowed. Private cars and routine through-traffic need to be gone. Let essential movement flow on the nearby avenues (Seventh Ave., Sixth Ave., Eighth Ave.) while the main plaza is made into a civic space. Not just a pedestrian oasis trapped in an island of machines.

It's not just about looks. Less crashes. Less air pollution. Less noise. Safer crossings. Important things in a city where children and seniors, employees and visitors, all jostle for space. And one of the few places in the world with symbolic value to make a statement: New York values people over easy car trips through midtown.

Let the city build on what started in 2009 by 2030. Let Times Square be first and foremost a space for the people who walk and work and perform and breathe life into the square. There are plenty of streets for cars to drive on. Let a square have some breathing room.

We need to have a car-free Times Square by 2030. Not as a gimmick, but as the logical extension of New York's longstanding effort to appropriate the city's public spaces for better purposes.

It started in 2009 during Mayor Michael Bloomberg's administration. Broadway was closed to cars through Times Square, and temporary pedestrian plazas were set up between 42nd and 47th Streets. It seemed so radical. And then it started to feel so normal. These pedestrian plazas cut down on vehicle interactions, increased the space available for pedestrians. Added tables, performances, or just the ability to stand still in one of the most vibrant places in the world.

So Times Square is an oxymoron. It's a place meant to overwhelm the senses. One of the most concentrated human spaces in the world—millions of people visiting every year. And yet there are still cars and trucks running through it. Over 300k pedestrians daily. They're negotiating between barricades, delivery trucks, taxis, buses, and turning cars. All while looking up at ads that sell New York City as the land of opportunity.

Making Times Square car-free all the time does not mean no vehicles at all. Emergency vehicles, work vehicles, accessibility vehicles, and planned deliveries can still make it through. But no private cars, no through traffic. The surrounding avenues like Seventh, Sixth, Eighth Avenue, can still serve as veins to accommodate needed traffic. The central plaza can be the true public space and not just some pedestrian oasis surrounded by a bunch of machines.

This isn't just a pretty argument. There's less air pollution, fewer accidents, less noise, and better pedestrian crossings. It's important in a city where we all walk around. Children, the elderly, workers, and tourists. We're all sharing a limited amount of space. And Times Square is one of the only places on this planet that has enough symbolism to make a point. New York City values the people more than the ease of driving through midtown.

So by 2030, we should see the conclusion of what started back in 2009. Let's make Times Square first and foremost for the people walking through it, the workers in it, the performers on it. For it's life. Because there's plenty of roads for cars. Let's let this one square breathe.

essay_opinion_03_glm.text:
I stumbled across a letter last march, lodged in a copy of Joan Didion’s “The White Album” that my mother sent me in 2019. A three-pager, all handwritten, 10/14/2019. It’s a report on the neighbor’s dog, and tomato prices in the Saturday farmers’ market in Davis, CA. Concerns that I wasn’t getting enough sleep in my Brooklyn flat. Cursive handwriting. Tilted and tiny. Apparently I’d read it and sent her a thumbs-up text.

That thumbs up has been bugging me.

I’m not nostalgic. I’m an iMessage freak. Yesterday I sent 47 texts. Mostly jokes. Mostly good. What a miracle the speed of digital communication. I wouldn’t give it up. But I’ve come to feel the handwritten letter is a space unto itself. We’ve sort of surrendered this space without realizing it.

The letter is an investment. There’s a sacrifice on the part of the letter writer. Maybe it took my mom 40 min to write those three pages. Time is the one thing you can’t return or regift. Handwritten letters reveal the sacrifice. Those slightly pinched lines by the margin: I kept writing. A text is: I thought of you for 4 seconds. Sometimes that’s fine. But not always.

And there’s the material reality of the letter. It made its way, in an envelope, through sorting facilities, across the country, to a blue mailbox on Fifth Ave. To my flat. My mother’s physical hand on the actual paper. I re-read it after she passed last June. I could almost feel the pressure of the pen. Where’s the emoji for that?

So I began writing her back before it was too late. And continued. Writing my friend Dana in Portland, my former prof in Chicago. One page a month, tops. That’s the key. The constraint is on the content. You can’t get away with a paragraph on the neighbor’s dog in handwriting without it mattering. Because your wrist will know when to stop. And your heart, made to slow down to the speed of the pen… well. Your heart will say what your thumb never would.

We don’t have a shortage of words. We have a shortage of slowness. The letter is slowness you can hold.

Last March I discovered this letter tucked away inside a copy of Joan Didion's The White Album. My mom sent me this book in 2019. I just discovered it now. It's three pages long. It's handwritten. It's dated October 14, of that year. It's her little angular italic cursive. It's about the neighbor's dog. Tomatoes at the Saturday market in Davis CA. How I'm not getting enough sleep in my Brooklyn apartment.

I apparently glanced at it and texted her 👍🏾

The 👍🏾 is like a dagger stuck in my soul.

I am not nostalgic. I love iMessage. I exchanged 47 texts yesterday. Mostly jokes. Mostly funny. Digital communication is miraculous in its speed. I wouldn't want to give that up.

But I think there is something we've given up without realizing it, without noticing, that can't be replaced by anything else. A hand-written letter.

I think there's something about a letter that makes it an expenditure for the person who writes it. My mom took probably 40 minutes to write those three pages. Time is the only thing you can't return or re-gift. And there's something about handwriting that makes it clear that there's been an expenditure. Each slightly cramped-on-the-margin line says, well, I went ahead anyway.

A text just says, I spent 4 seconds thinking about you. Which is sometimes enough.

But it's not always enough.

And there's something about a physical thing. That letter has been in an envelope. Through sorting rooms. Cross country. A blue box in New York, Fifth Ave. Up to my apartment. My mom's hand was on that real paper. And then last June when she died I re-read that letter and I felt the pressure of that pen almost. Can you show me the emoji for that.

So I tried to write back before it was too late for her. And I've tried to keep at it since. To my friend Dana in Portland. My old professor in Chicago. One page a month max. That's the point.

What you're limited to is the content. You can't write a paragraph about the neighbor's dog by hand without it feeling like it means something. Because you're wrist will know when you've written enough. And because your heart will slow down with the speed of the pen and say things you never would with a thumb.

It's not that we don't have enough words. It's that we don't have enough slowness.

A letter is like a slowness you can hold.

essay_opinion_05_sonnet.text:
My dad bought a Corolla in June of 1998 (4 months before I was born). It’s still running fine with 214,000 miles. It was from a Toyota dealer in Fresno that no longer exists. It still uses a cassette for music. There’s an old JCPenney receipt stuck in the map pocket (it’s been there since 2003) no one’s bothered to take out (superstition).

I pay $94.97 a month for stuff that doesn’t exist in any physical space. Spotify. ICloud. ChatGPT plus. I have a meditation app. I opened it 4 times. I have New York Times sub for the crossword. Adobe. Vpn. Amazon prime (which to me is not a subscription but more like a tax now). None of this stuff depreciates like a car does. None of it will exist (in a form I’d recognize) by the time the Corolla is of age to pay its own subscription bills in 2054.

You have to care for the Corolla in a particular way. My dad will change the oil himself every 5000 miles. In the driveway. Using a bucket older than I am. When things break, he knows what the part is. Timing belt. Knock sensor. He has opinions on NGK vs Denso spark plugs. The relationship is 100% but it’s importantly over. When he turned over the keys, the sale was done. He has a thing. The thing is not owed any more to him.

The things I have are owed an endless amount of maintenance in a different currency. The terms of service have shifted. They quietly move from $9.99 to $12.99 with an email I never read. They deprecate the thing I liked. And replace it with something that needs a higher tier to have. I’m not maintaining anything. I’m being maintained on, silently by 14 different companies that think they have priority access to my attention and debit card. Corolla needs oil every few thousand miles. My subscriptions need something different, more regular. Need me to glance over at it. To log in. To renew without my realizing until my bank statement alerts me.

Used to think it’s just ownership vs access. But it’s more like: The car my dad has is “worsening” in ways he can anticipate and address. My software is “improving” in ways I didn’t want and can’t escape. He’s still driving the same thing he was in 2004. It’s not like I’m still using the same Spotify in 2019. The UI. The algo. The price point. Everything changed subtly under the same name.

He’s gonna drive that thing til it dies. I don’t think I can ever say that about anything I’m paying a monthly subscription for.

He's driving the same car he was in 2004. I'm not using the same spotify I was in 2019. Interface. Algorithm. Price. Quietly replaced. All under the same 4 letters.

What Every City Should Do Like Bogota Does Ciclovía Sundays

Not as a gimmick. Not as an anomaly. As a civic dream to have once a week.

Once a week in Bogotá, on Sundays and public holidays, they close about 140 kilometers of roads to cars, from 7am to 2pm. Instead of cars, the streets are full of cyclists, joggers, inline skaters, strollers, old people on foot. Streets and avenues that are normally for driving. This began on December 15, 1974, when a small citizen movement blocked a few of the main streets. Today, 50 years later, one may say that on an average week over a million people might use the system.

The beauty of Ciclovía is that it seems like a very modest thing to ask. You don't need to build an extension of the subway or a new stadium or a fleet of futuristic electric buses. All you need are some barricades. Some traffic cops. Some toilets. Some first aid posts. The political audacity to say, this is seven hours where movement and pleasure trump parking.

I can recall watching for the first time the video of Bogotá's Carrera Séptima on a Sunday. It didn't look like an avenue of transit. It looked more like a living room. Wobbly kids on bikes. Adolescents doing tricks. Grandparents holding hands. Juice and arepa vendors. It's not that the city built a new park. It's that they gave back the old one to the people: the street.

This is important. Urban policy tends to be focused on commuting. How fast do people get to the center. How many cars can we cram at a corner. How efficient can we make the flow of things. With Ciclovía there is a new use for the city. Being in it for its own sake. Not having to purchase. Or to go somewhere.

Of course it's a disruption to close a street. People will complain. Of course it is. It's the job of the city to find ways of balancing things. Not to pretend cars are the only valid actors in public space. Also, you can test this easily with a Sunday closure. Let people see what a calm, safe street would be like. Before we even start arguing about redesigning something.

In any city you could do this incrementally. One avenue. Four hours. One Sunday a month. And see what happens. People will come. Not because you told them to work out. But because you invited them to be there.

Every city should emulate Bogotá’s Ciclovía Sundays, not as a gimmick but as a weekly exercise in collective imagination.

Every Sunday and holiday, Bogota blocks about 140 kilometers of streets to traffic between 7 am and 2 pm. Bikes, joggers, skaters, baby strollers, and old people on foot claim avenues that are otherwise the preserve of cars. It started on December 15, 1974 when a group of citizens organized a small protest blocking off some of the city’s main streets. A half century later, it may attract over a million people during an average week.

The brilliance of Ciclovía is that it doesn’t need much. You don’t need to build a subway extension or a new sports stadium or a futuristic fleet of electric buses. What you need are barricades, traffic cops, porta potties, first-aid stations, and political guts to assert that for seven hours of the week, mobility and enjoyment trump parking.

The first time I saw video of Bogotá’s Carrera Séptima on a Sunday morning, it struck me that this isn’t just another thoroughfare but a living room. Kids wobble on bikes. Kids do tricks. Grandparents stroll side by side. Juice and arepa vendors hawk their wares. You didn’t build a new park, you gave back the one you already had—the street—to the people.

This is crucial. Most urban policy is oriented toward the commute—how fast workers can travel downtown, how many cars we can fit at an intersection, how fast we can transport goods. With Ciclovía, we consider the alternative use—being in the city without having to buy anything or go anywhere.

Critics will argue that closing streets is disruptive. Of course it is! Cities are supposed to balance demands, not act like cars are the only valid occupants of public space. And closing a street on Sundays is an inexpensive experiment. It gives people a taste of what it would be like to have a calmer, safer street before we even get into any talk of permanent street redesign.

Start small. Block off one avenue for four hours on one Sunday each month. See what happens. People will show up. Not because they’re being told to exercise, but because they’re being invited to be a part.

I have been going to the Met since I was nine and my grandmother gave me a couple of dollars and we stayed in the Egyptian section of the museum for the entire afternoon. That's what the place was for. So that kids from Queens could come and stand before a Temple of Dendur and feel like all of history was theirs.

But now it's increasingly expensive to feel that way. In August 2022 the museum increased the mandatory fee for visitors who are not residents of New York State from $25 to $30. Next, in 2025, they bumped it up to $35. Which is one of the highest museum fees in the country. You can pay whatever you can afford, theoretically, if you live in New York State, but this requires a considerable fine print. All the kiosks advertise the higher price first. You need to know the trick to take advantage of it. And you need to be prepared to say it to an employee that you would like to pay $1. If you're a family of four from the Bronx, it's not a bargain, it's an audition.

The museum's leadership explains the increase by simple economics. The increased post-pandemic expenses. The insurance. The climate control of the two million items in the museum. Sure, the museum's endowment isn't as robust as it was. But let's be clear about who they're asking to make up the difference. It's not the galas-going trustees. It's not the tourists whose $35 is a mere drop in the bucket compared to their $600 hotel stay. It's the group of teenagers from Newark on a field trip. It's the nanny who has her day off. It's the art student who would come on Tuesdays to draw.

What it means for a city is the level of access its lowest income citizens have. The park, Central Park, is free. The ferry to Staten Island is free. The Met was to be like that. A public institution on public land. Leased from the city. Subsidized by public funds. $35 entry fee tells you that culture is a product. And you are a consumer.

It's actually very simple. British Museum and the Tate in London have maintained free entry through many more economic crises than we're experiencing now. Because access has been deemed essential in the UK. And the museum can go after that. The endowment drives. City support. Rather than furtively making its museum inaccessible to the very people who it should belong to.

Otherwise, soon, there will be a nine-year-old girl from Queens who will come to stand before those steps on Fifth Avenue. And her grandmother will see the ticket price and walk on. The Met will be worse off for it. As will the city.

I love a farmers market. Every Saturday, north end of Marion Park in Cleveland - twelve tents - dude who sells honey (hives in Bedford Heights) - lady selling heirloom tomatoes that make your steak look cheap.

But it's almost beside the point. Six blocks south of that park is an area we've labeled Central. We haven't had a full-scale grocery store here since a Dave's closed in 2013. Just two dollar stores, Marathon, market that mainly sells cigs and lottery tickets behind bulletproof glass. If you want a head of broccoli that hasn't been under a fluorescent light since March, you've got to drive, or take 6 bus for 90 minutes round trip, or pay $4.50 for a bag of shriveled carrots at corner store. Last USDA food access mapping: 12,000 people in that area, mostly don't have cars.

People are going to talk about these farmers markets as the solution. And sure - they're great. They're photogenic, easy to point a camera at, easy for city councilor to do a ribbon cutting in front of. But a farmers market that is there 4 hours/week seasonally - cash optional, produce aimed at folks who already eat well - is not infrastructure. It's a supplement. Not something you can base your diet on if it only takes SNAP if you remembered to bring the token thing Saturday 9-1 May - October.

The way you solve a food desert isn't very exciting. It's a grocery store with butcher counter and pharmacy, every day of the week. With parking or bus stop outside. With $2 rice and $3 dozen eggs, not $9 microgreens. And it's an expensive process to re-establish that. You need tax abatements, city loans. Sometimes someone gets paid to take the risk, like Pittsburgh did w/ Hill District Shop n Save in 2013 with $10.8M in public financing. It's not as quick, or telegenic, as a farmers market ribbon cutting. But it's what feeds your neighborhood on Tuesday in February, when there's no market, no tent, no honey guy - just what's on the shelf in walking distance.

The farmer's market that happens on the northern part of Marion Park every Saturday in Cleveland, 12 tents, guy selling honey from his hives in Bedford Heights, lady selling heirloom tomatoes that cost more than a steak. I'm into it. And I'm also into it being kind of a sideshow. 
 If you want a broccoli head not sitting under fluorescent lights since March, you've got to have a car or take 6 bus 90 minutes round-trip, or be ok with $4.50 bag of old wrinkly carrots at the corner store. We've dubbed the area south of that park 6 blocks away 'central' because they haven't had a full-service grocery store there since a Dave's shut down in 2013. Just two dollar stores, a Marathon gas station and a market selling mostly cigarettes and lottery tickets behind bulletproof glass. 12,000+ people live in between. Last USDA food access mapping says that. Mostly no cars. 
 They push the farmers market thing as the answer to this. And I get why. They're visible and pretty and easy to do a ribbon cutting in front of as a city council guy. But a farmers market that's 4 hours a week seasonally, with no card required and priced for people who already eat well. That's not infrastructure. That's an add on. You can't base a diet on a farmers market that's open Saturday 9-1, May-October, and takes SNAP only if you happen to bring the token machine with you. 
 The way you close a food desert is lame. Grocery store. One with a butcher and pharmacy. Open every day. Parking or a bus stop out front. With $2 rice and $3/dozen eggs. Not $9 microgreens. That takes $$. Tax abatements, city loans. Sometimes paying a grocer to eat the risk. Like Pittsburgh did with the Hill district Shop 'n Save in 2013. Gave them $10.8mm in public money. Not as easy, fast or pretty as doing a ribbon cutting for a farmers market. But also the way you feed a neighborhood in Central when it's Tuesday and February. No farmers market. No tent. No honey guy. Just whatever's in walking distance on the shelf.

My 9-year-old daughter Maya just had a birthday in March, and instead of giving her a smartphone, I got her a flip phone.

This is a beat-up purple Nokia. It has a plastic case with scratches and a tiny screen and a battery that just doesn’t seem to die. She uses it to call me when her soccer practice is over early at Lincoln Elementary. She uses it to text her grandma in Sacramento. She uses it to check in when she’s walking 3 blocks from our apartment to the library on Saturdays. That’s basically it.

It’s not that I’m against technology. Maya’s already swimming in technology. She’s got a school Chromebook. She’s watching science videos. She knows how to ask Alexa for the weather. It’s this specific kind of technology that I’m trying to delay for a bit. And this specific kind of technology is a smartphone. It’s that endless flow of notifications and videos and games and ads and social comparisons and adult attention.

Maya’s 9. She’s still figuring out how to be bored. When she’s on the bus on her way to her swimming lessons, she looks out the window. She notices the mural on 14th Street. She notices the guy with oranges by the station. She notices if she can see the moon through the buildings. She figured out how to do a card trick last week. She spent 20 minutes trying to figure it out by herself because she had nothing to do. I don’t want to just fill all the space for her until she sees what might be possible there.

The flip phone also gives communication a little more… intent. When Maya calls, she’s trying to say something. And when I call, she’ll say, “Hi, Dad.” Not just looking down at a screen and still playing the game. We’ve got a family rule that you keep your phone in your backpack when you’re eating. So her phone is usually shut off by 7:30 pm. I don’t have to moderate a group chat. Or keep an eye on a social media account. Or explain to her why someone in her class has 400 likes on their vacation video.

It’s also kind of annoying, to have a flip phone. She can’t easily share pictures. Or use maps. Or message her friends using the app that everyone else is using. Sometimes she complains that she’s the only 4th grader without an iPhone. I tell her “not yet” is a complete answer.

She will get a smartphone. But for now, I want her first phone to be a tool for her independence. Not a mobile internet-in-a-box.

I still recall the purchase price of my first album I purchased with my own money. Tower Records, Sunset blvd. April 2003. $14.99. Radiohead, "Hail to the Thief." I listened to it so much that summer that I recall the seams between "2 + 2 = 5" and "Sit Down. Stand Up." How it ran from one to the other.

You know what we miss? We miss the money, sure (14-year-olds, $14.99 = money). But we miss the seam. The run. The decision of the band.

Streaming gave us everything — 100 million+ songs on Spotify as of 2024 — but as a consequence, it made sequencing meaningless. Music became infinite. Playlist became algorithmic slot machine. Spotify's Discover Weekly hits you with 30 songs every Monday. As studies indicate, most listeners abandon any given song in five to thirty seconds. We don't listen to songs. We sample. All the time. Forever.

An album was an argument. "The End" is the climax of Abbey Road. OK Computer: "Fitter Happier" in the right place. Dead-eyed gap between "Karma Police" and "Electioneering." Even a mixtape. I made a ton in HS. Laboriously, on the Sony dual deck. A testament to care. What came after what? Sequencing was the point. You could read people's souls from the distance between their Radiohead song and the Björk one they followed.

Now, shuffle's the default. "Enhance" adds songs the machine thinks are suitable. Skip-skip-skip. The average Spotify listener plays ~40 songs in a given week, over and over, even though we have an infinite library. Infinite choice? It narrowed our tastes. Not broadened them.

I don't want to be nostalgic. Streaming is a miracle, in many respects. A kid from Fresno can listen to Fela and Fugazi in the same afternoon. For free. But there was a cost to abundance. Music went from an act of commitment to an ambient force. Like weather. Songs were events. Now they're ambiance.

My little act of rebellion: every Friday night, listen to a whole album start to finish. No phone. No skipping. Last week, it was Alvvays "Blue Rev." That 51 minutes felt more like listening than the last six months.

We miss the seams. Forgot to notice when we lost 'em.

I remember the cost of the first record I purchased. $14.99. Tower Records on Sunset Blvd in April of 2003. Radiohead, _Hail to the Thief_. Played it so much all summer I still hear the seam between '2 + 2 = 5' and 'Sit Down. Stand Up'. You know what? The specific seam. The flow from one song to the next.

We've lost that. Not the money (alright $14.99 is something when you're 14), we've lost the seam. We've lost the transition. The decision by the band about what comes next.

With all this music. Streaming. 100 million plus tracks on Spotify in 2024. It made it meaningless.

When there's unlimited music the playlist becomes a machine. An algorithm slot machine. Every Monday morning Spotify throws thirty songs in your ears. Most people, according to research, skip the track after 5-30 seconds.

We don't listen to songs anymore. We sample. All the time. Forever.

An album was an argument. _Abbey Road_ ends with 'The End'. _OK Computer_ puts 'Fitter Happier' where it needs to be. A blinkered intermission between 'Karma Police' and 'Electioneering'. A mixtape, I made dozens in high school. With care. Sony dual deck cassette. Toiling.

The mixtape showed an investment. You cared about the order. The message is in the order. It's readable. Someone could interpret your soul by seeing the distance between Radiohead and the Bjork song you followed it with.

The queue defaults to a shuffle now. 'Enhance' it adds tracks the machine deems appropriate. Skip. Skip. Skip. Average Spotify listener loops a few dozen songs over and over, even with the seemingly infinite music (infinite choice equaled a narrowing of taste).

I'm not Nostalgia Man. There's so many wonders about streaming. A kid in Fresno can listen to Fela Kuti and Fugazi in the same afternoon. All for free.

But there's a silent cost. The music went from a commitment to a passing thing. Like the weather. We don't have events. Now it's all ambient.

So my little resistance: every Friday night. One full album. Start to finish. No phone. No skip. Last week was _Blue Rev_ by Alvvays. More of a listening experience for 51 minutes than the last six months.

The seams. We forgot to see when they left.

Tuesdays I'm usually at the Enoch Pratt Free Library, Cathedral Street, in Baltimore. 
 Never have I been asked to pay for access. 
 A shocking statement? Should not be. If you sit in any open space for 3 hours in the US: A coffee shop, a mall food court, the hotel lobby. 
 How long until you're asked what you're buying? 
 The library is one of the last places where the cost of entry is 0, and the service agreement is simple: be a person. 
 Enoch Pratt doesn't ask you your zip code. LA Public Library's 73 branches don't ask you about your immigration status. Brooklyn Public Library gave away 6600 free digital library cards to teens around the country in 2022 after a surge in book banning. So Texas/Florida kids could read the books banned in their local libraries. 
 So what's left? Maybe a park bench, until some city adds those armrests that prevent you from laying down. (500+ instances of hostile architecture have been documented across major US cities since 2014). 
 Maybe a church (if you go). 
 Maybe the DMV (public but not really a place you hang out). 
 Everything's been remetered. 
 The mall has become a place you get watched by private security guards who are on the property owner's payroll. 
 The sidewalk cafe is a $7 espresso cover charge. 
 Even the internet (the great equalizer of our time) is now fueled by data brokers selling your library-esque google searches to advertisers. 
 Libraries are fueled by the Library Bill of Rights. First passed by the American Library Association in 1939.  
 It still states that there shouldn't be any restrictions in the type of materials available, due to the background or opinions of people contributing to their creation. 
 This is no accident. 
 Andrew Carnegie financed 1689 library buildings in the US from 1883-1929. 
 But only if the town committed to using public taxes to ensure that these libraries would be free forever. 
 He recognized (more than most robber barons) that rooms for democracy exist, where you are not asked to pay rent to maintain citizenship. 
 61% of Americans visited a library (or library website) in the past year per Pew 2024 survey. More than voted in the last midterm. 
 This isn't nostalgia. It's the last commons. 
 Let's not miss it.

Most Tuesdays, I visit the Enoch Pratt Free Library on Cathedral St in Baltimore. And not once has anyone ever asked me to pay for a stay.

That shouldn't seem unusual, but try sitting for three hours in any public space here in America. Coffee shop, food court in a mall, hotel lobby. How long before someone asks you what are you buying? The library is one of the last rooms in America where the cost to enter is nothing. The TOS is: be a person. Enoch Pratt won't ask you for your zip. The LA Public Library has 73 locations where they don't ask for your immigration status. The Brooklyn Public Library gave 6,600 free digital library cards to teens around the country in 2022, following book bans. So kids in Texas or Florida could access books they weren't seeing at their libraries anymore.

So what's left? Perhaps a park bench, until some city puts the armrests that prohibit anyone from laying down. (There are over 500 cases of hostile architecture in major cities in the US documented since 2014.) Maybe a church (if you have one). Or DMV. (It's public, but no one really hangs out there.) Everything else has just been remetered. Mall = a place where you'll be surveilled by security guards on the owner's dime. Sidewalk Cafe = we'll let you hang out here for $7 espresso. Even the Internet, once the great equalizer, now comes thanks to data brokers that will sell your library adjacent Google searches to marketers. But libraries? Run by the Library Bill of Rights (first adopted by the American Library Association in 1939). Which still says that stuff shouldn't be excluded based on the origin or views of those who have contributed to the creation of the materials.

This is no accident. Andrew Carnegie paid for 1,689 libraries buildings in the US between 1883 and 1929. But only if towns committed to using public tax money for those libraries to remain free forever. Carnegie knew, unlike most robber barons, that democracy requires places where you don't need to pay rent on your citizenship.

61% of Americans used a library or library website in the last year. (Pew 2024). More than voted in the last midterm. It's not about nostalgia. It's the last commons. Notice that before it's not.

In William Shakespeare's Macbeth, Act 5, Scene 1 Lady Macbeth's guilt is evident through her sleepwalking, constant hand-washing, and her deranged speech. Contrastingly, Lady Macbeth seemed very bold and unremorseful at the beginning of the play when she suggested Macbeth to kill King Duncan at Inverness following the feast at Act 1. Now in Act 5, Lady Macbeth is entirely consumed by her own guilty conscience. At the beginning of the scene, the Doctor and the Gentlewoman witness Lady Macbeth coming in with a candle, as if Lady Macbeth is scared of the dark, so afraid of the evils that she, herself, has helped commit. Despite the fact that Lady Macbeth is in a dream, she is actually talking about experiencing the murder of Duncan, Banquo, and Lady Macduff. Lady Macbeth speaks the phrase, 'Out, damned spot!' This phrase is showing that she sees herself with blood on her hands. Even though there is no 'spot' on her hands, there is a psychological spot of never-ending guilt for the murder of Duncan. Earlier Lady Macbeth believed that, 'a little water clears us of this deed.' This implies that we can easily wash away guilt just as we can easily wipe away the blood off of our skin. However, at Act 5, Scene 1, it is clear that guilt is not easily washed away.

It is also evident through Lady Macbeth's speech that she has clear recollection of the crimes they had committed. In her speech she says, 'Who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him?' This is clearly referring to Duncan, whom she once saw as a practical issue concerning murder. She also cries, 'The Thane of Fife had a wife; where is she now?' This is a reminder of Lady Macduff's death whom she ordered to be killed by Macbeth's orders. Through this recollection of memories, it is clear that Lady Macbeth is not only feeling guilty about the crimes she committed but she is also feeling guilty about the blood shed throughout the time of Macbeth's rule. It is clarified by the Gentlewoman that Lady Macbeth has been washing her hands for 15 minutes now. This shows the extent of guilty that has affected her both mentally and physically. Unlike Macbeth, who is overcome by fear, and instead orders more murders to be committed, Lady Macbeth is consumed by the consequences of their ambitious actions. The guilt she feels, causes her to be isolated from the court, and even from Macbeth, who is now battling with the oncoming English troops, led by Malcolm at the vicinity of Dunsinane Castle. Thus, Shakespeare shows that Lady Macbeth's guilty is a moral fate that cannot be avoided. Even though she once thought that she could be above conscience, the blood she has helped shed has scarred her mental health forever.

In Act 5, scene 1, Lady Macbeth displays her feelings of guilt through her sleepwalking, her constant hand-washing, and her disjointed speech. In earlier scenes of the play Lady Macbeth was very bold and even callous, telling Macbeth to kill King Duncan in Inverness after the feast at Act 1. By Act 5, Lady Macbeth is completely overwhelmed by her conscience. The Doctor and the Gentlewoman notice her entering the room with a candle. It seems Lady Macbeth is terrified of the darkness, tormented by the atrocities she has helped to instigate. Though Lady Macbeth is asleep, she seems to be reliving the murder of Duncan, Banquo, and Lady Macduff. She exclaims, "Out, damned spot!" imagining that there is blood on her hands. Though there is no real "spot" on her hands physically, this "spot" represents the deep, abiding guilt she feels over the murder of Duncan. She had previously said that "a little water clears us of this deed", but clearly, as evidenced by Scene 1, guilt is not as simple to wash away as blood off the skin.

Lady Macbeth's speech indicates that she remembers the specific details of these crimes. For example, she says, "Who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him?" She is speaking of Duncan, the man whom she once considered a practical problem to be dealt with. Also, she screams, "The Thane of Fife had a wife; where is she now?" This is Lady Macduff, who was slain by Lady Macbeth's order at Macbeth's direction. These memories show that Lady Macbeth's guilt extends not only to her own deeds, but to the bloody actions that occurred throughout Macbeth's reign of terror. The Gentlewoman points out that Lady Macbeth has been washing her hands for fifteen minutes, underscoring the extent to which Lady Macbeth's guilt has affected her mentally and physically. Lady Macbeth, in contrast to Macbeth, who uses fear as an excuse to cause more murders, is totally undone by the effects of their ambition. Her guilt keeps her separate from court, even from Macbeth who is battling the incoming English army, under Malcolm's command, near Dunsinane Castle. The point of Lady Macbeth's guilt, as written by Shakespeare, is that this guilt is the inescapable, moral retribution for her crimes. Although she thought herself above conscience, the blood she instigated has left a permanent scar on her mind.

Though often underestimated, the introduction of the Ford Model A in December 1927 was a big factor in pushing the development of American suburbs forward in the late 1920s and 1930s. When the old Ford Model T finally ceased production in May 1927, the Ford company closed down its plants for half a year to be retooled. On December 2, 1927, the new Ford Model A was released. Suddenly, Americans had a car that was faster, safer, and more comfortable than the Model T had been. Starting at around $385 for the Model A Roadster and up to around $1400 for the Model A Town Car, the Model A was still quite affordable to middle class families. In October 1973, OPEC countries in the Middle East, upset over US backing of Israel during the Yom Kippur war, decided to reduce the output of oil and place an embargo on the US, Netherlands and other Western allies. The price of a barrel of oil quadrupled in just a few months - by early 1974, it had gone from around $3 to almost $12. The shock made clear, starkly, how reliant Western nations had become on a resource they didn't control.

Even as a major oil producer, the US had reached its peak of domestic production in 1970, and by 1973 imported around a third of its oil. For Western Europe and Japan, the dependence was even greater - they imported the bulk of their oil from the Middle East and North Africa. The impact of the embargo was fast and clear: in the US, gasoline rationing. Odd-even license plate systems to dictate when you could buy gas. Lines at the pump. A national speed limit of 55 miles per hour introduced in early 1974 to conserve fuel. In the UK, the oil shock and a strike in the coal mines led the government to impose a three-day work week in industry. In Japan, where over 75% of the country's energy was imported, the oil shock triggered panic buying for consumer goods and inflation - dubbed the "toilet paper panic" of 1973.

The economic effects were deep and long-lasting. Inflation in the US rose over 12% by 1974. Stock markets crashed. The age of cheap energy that had been the cornerstone of post-war prosperity was over. Economists started talking about "stagflation" - the now all too common mix of economic stagnation and inflation. And they found that traditional economic policies were unable to fix the problem.

But the embargo had another effect - it provoked a reckoning. Western countries set up the International Energy Agency in 1974 to manage emergency oil stocks and minimize dependence. In France, they started a massive nuclear power programme. In Japan, they put a lot of effort into energy efficiency and became a world leader in energy efficient technologies. Denmark started moving towards wind power. So the crisis wasn't just about dependence - it was also about how to change.

The oil embargo of 1973 is a classic example of economic interdependence. A cartel of oil producers could use their resource as a political weapon and almost instantly destabilize the world's most prosperous economies. It showed that energy security was national security. And that has a strong impact on foreign policy - from the strategic oil reserve to debates today about renewable energy and supply chains. The gas station queues of 1973 weren't just a nuisance - they were a warning the West has never really forgotten.

In October 1973, OPEC (Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries) member nations from the Arab world, upset by US support for Israel in the Yom Kippur War, reduced oil production and instituted an oil embargo against the US, the Netherlands, and other allies. By a few months later, oil prices had quadrupled from around $3 to almost $12 by early 1974. The 1973 oil shock forcefully revealed the extent to which the Western world had become dependent on a resource it had no control over.

Although the US is a significant oil producer, US oil production peaked in 1970, and the US imported around one-third of its oil in 1973. Western Europe and Japan were much more reliant on oil imports, with the majority of their petroleum imported from the Middle East and North Africa. The oil embargo immediately produced results and became obvious. In the US, people saw gas rationing, odd and even license plates for fueling on different days, gas lines, and, in early 1974, a national speed limit of 55 mph to save fuel. Britain had to introduce a 3-day working week for industry due to the oil shock and a coal miners' strike. In Japan, which imported more than 75% of its energy, people panicked and began buying up consumer goods, causing inflation. This was known as the "Toilet paper panic" of 1973.

The economic consequences were considerable and prolonged. In the US, inflation exceeded 12% in 1974, stock markets plunged, and the age of cheap energy supporting postwar growth and prosperity ended. Economists talked about "stagflation," the unusual combination of slow growth and inflation. The standard policies appear to be inadequate.

The oil embargo forced people to think about dependence and consider solutions. The International Energy Agency was formed in 1974 for coordination and emergency supplies to reduce dependence. France started a large nuclear power program. Japan began investing in energy efficiency and became a global leader in fuel efficiency technology. The Danes started their transition to wind power. It was a time of dependence and showed what can be done.

The 1973 oil embargo was a key example of how dependent we are on others. A group of producers can wield their resource as political leverage and cause turmoil in the richest economies in the world almost instantly. Energy security is national security. It's a lesson that continues to influence foreign policy decisions. From the strategic petroleum reserve to current discussions about renewable energy and supply chains. The long gas lines of 1973 were more than just an inconvenience. It was a warning that the West has never completely ignored.

I remember in September of 2022, how my mom had to go through and think our grocery list through 3 times at the Kroger off Elm Street before adding anything to the cart. It was in September of 2022 that the Bureau of Labor Statistics had proven what my family and I had been feeling for weeks leading up to it - inflation was running around 9.1% YoY, the highest rate in 40 years. For my family of 5 in a mid-sized Ohio suburb, the 9.1% number wasn't some abstract metric on the evening news anymore. It was a deeply individual line item negotiation of what we were able to afford to eat anymore.

In years prior, my mom's typical weekly grocery trip cost us around $180 and required 2 carts. come October of 2022 the exact same list now was running closer to $240 and she'd have to edit the list to fit into 1 cart. Egg prices that were $1.50/dozen at the time had skyrocketed to over $3.50 after an avian flu broke out and drove inflation even higher. Milk prices had risen from $2.80/gallon to almost $4.20/gallon. Ground Beef, a normal Tuesday night meal, was replaced by lentils and canned beans from a Sam's Club bulk membership my father reluctantly acquired after years of resistance. He had ground beef once a week instead of 5 nights/week.

We found our ways around it in little calculated ways. My mom had gone from a name brand cereal to the same brand Kroger ones which saved us about $1.20/box for cereal. My younger brother, 12 at the time, couldn't get the individually packaged snack packs he liked for school lunches anymore. The cost per unit had nearly doubled. We got a small veggie garden this last spring with tomatoes, peppers, and zucchini. This was less of a fun hobby and more a way to prepare for the nearly 8% increase of produce costs that year.

It was the way that the numbers changed the conversations that I found interesting more than anything. Dinner planning, something we had previously maybe thought about somewhat, was now a Sunday night budgeting meeting with the calculator on the kitchen table. My parents were looking at receipts from Kroger and Aldi and Meijer and even putting in the 15 extra minutes of drive to Aldi. Even $15 extra a week mattered.

Come early 2023 prices had stopped rising as quickly but had also stopped dropping. Our $240 grocery bill was the new status quo. Not because we were used to it, but because we had nothing to go back to. 2022 was the year of learning how inflation wasn't just a number, but how it silently eats away at your choices as a family that you've been used to.
