It's unethical to advertise to kids under 12 because young kids don't understand the difference between persuasion and information. The American Academy of Pediatrics reported in 2020 that kids under the age of 8 usually don't understand the intent of advertisements. That means they're especially susceptible to ads for sweet cereal, toys, video games, fast food etc. For instance, a 6 year old might think a cartoon character promoting a sugary, colorful cereal is just giving them a recommendation for a fun product, not realizing the cereal company paid for it to try to sell more of their product.

It's especially unethical when ads use personal data and digital technology. In 2019 Google settled for $170M with the Federal Trade Commission and New York Attorney General for allegedly gathering children's personal data on YouTube without the proper parental consent. Even when ads aren't gathering data, some online games can blur the lines between marketing and play. Kids may not realize a game reward, influencer video, or "unboxing" promotion is aimed to push them into buying something.

That's not to say all ads to kids should be outlawed. Ads could be educating kids about books, learning programs, sports equipment, or even healthier foods. And ads help companies employ people and keep competition going. But there are ethical boundaries because kids don't have the life experience, independence, or critical thinking skills that adults do. Companies shouldn't be marketing to kids using psychological manipulation, deceptive sponsorship, deceptive health benefits, or pushing them to try to convince their parents. They also shouldn't be gathering kids' data to target them with ads.

It's not all on parents to take care of this, especially when companies have teams of psychologists, designers, and data scientists working to target kids as consumers. A reasonable approach would include banning targeted ads to kids under 12. Labeling sponsored content. Limiting food ads for unhealthy food in kids' programs. Big fines for violations. It's not to remove kids' options, but to preserve their independence as it develops. An ethical approach to advertising would acknowledge that childhood is a time to learn and grow, and shouldn't just be thought of as a time to be a profitable consumer.

Children under the age of 12 are vulnerable targets for ethically questionable advertising because children this young struggle to separate advertising from information. As the American Academy of Pediatrics reported in 2020, children under the age of 8 tend to lack the awareness of the point of advertising. As a result, they are especially susceptible to commercials selling sugary cereals, toys, video games, and fast food. For example, a six-year-old might think that when a cartoon character is promoting a colorful cereal for breakfast, it's just because he likes the product. The child may not realize that the company paid to promote this in order to sell more product.

There are additional ethical concerns when advertising exploits personal information and takes advantage of digital media. For instance, Google reached a settlement to pay $170 million to the Federal Trade Commission and the New York Attorney General in 2019 after regulators charged that the company was using YouTube to collect personal information from children without adequate parental consent. Without even collecting data, advertisements can bleed into children's games, where a child might not even know that a prize within a game, an influencer's video, or an "unboxing" program are promoting sales.

Not all child-oriented advertisements are unethical. There are ads that can encourage reading books, learning in educational programs, participating in sports, or eating healthy foods. Advertisements are also important to businesses to provide employment and encourage competition. But ethics matter here because children are generally not as experienced, independent, or discerning as adults. It's unethical for companies to use manipulative methods, covert sponsorships, false health claims, or peer pressure to get kids to influence their parents. It's unethical to exploit kids' data to deliver personalized ads.

There are things parents should do, but it's not entirely fair to put it on parents while companies use teams of psychologists, designers, and data analysts to target children as consumers. In an ideal policy, it would be illegal to target children under 12 with ads. It would be required to clearly mark sponsored content. Advertising unhealthy foods during children's programming would be limited. And there would be substantial consequences for violations. The purpose is not to take away options from children, but to foster the growth of their independence. Ethical advertising would treat childhood as a time of learning and growth. It would not simply see children as valuable consumers.

Near the conclusion of Mark Twain's 'Adventures of Huckleberry Finn' (1884) Huck is put to the final test of his moral evolution: will he write the letter informing Miss Watson of Jim's (her run away slave's) whereabouts or go to "hell" and destroy the letter. Huck scratches out the note for the owner of Jim in Hannibal's St. Petersburg. For a fleeting instant he feels "washed clean of sin" but he recalls their thousand-mile journey down the Mississippi. The Cairo fog. Jim calling him "honey" and tending to him like a father. With the letter in his hand Huck shakes. He recollects his short prayer. And finally he says, "All right, then, I'll go to hell." And he rips the paper in two.

This is a crucial moment. Huck is not morally corrupt. His conscience is fractured by his society. He has been taught in Sunday school and by Widow Douglas that assisting an escape for a slave is stealing. It is damned. In this world doing the "right thing" is a disloyalty to a friend. And so Twain's irony is savage. At his most moral Huck feels himself to be a sinner. By opting for eternal damnation rather than re-enslavement for Jim Huck is not only rejecting the ownership rights of Miss Watson, but also a whole system of values. He evolves morally by learning to trust the "sound heart" of his experience rather than the "deformed conscience" of his culture. That's a phrase Twain used in an 1895 notebook to sum up the novel's main conflict.

Furthermore, Huck's choice is a victory of empathy over abstractions. He doesn't come to abolitionism through reason. He has no political ideology. But he remembers. He recalls Jim grieving for his daughter 'Lizabeth (he struck her before realizing she was deaf). He recalls Jim's happiness at seeing Huck alive after the feud with the Grangerfords. He recalls their quarrelling like a family over King Solomon and the French on the raft. Huck's ethics are a series of moments of shared humanity. Not a doctrine.

Of course the novel's final section in which Tom Sawyer turns the already-liberated Jim's release into a game undermines the process of Huck's evolution. But it does not nullify it. In choosing hell Huck reveals that conscience isn't a God-given compass given by society. It's something you build bit by bit out of loyalty and love. Huck doesn't evolve to be respectable. He evolves to be good.

When we read Mark Twain's 'Adventures of Huckleberry Finn' (1884) and get towards the conclusion, we reach the pivotal decision in Huck's moral journey: shall he write a letter to Miss Watson, informing her of Jim, her runaway slave, or 'go to hell' and burn it? As he scratches out the message for the owner of Jim in St. Petersburg, Hannibal, he feels a bit 'washed clean of sin', but then he thinks of the thousand miles they've floated on the Mississippi, the Cairo fog, Jim calling him 'honey' and treating him like a father. He holds the letter in his hand. He shivers. He recalls his short prayer. He finally pronounces, 'All right, then, I'll go to hell.' He rips it in half.

The reason this is important is because it's not Huck's own sin that has broken his conscience. It's his society. Huck's been taught in Sunday school and by Widow Douglas that helping someone escape slavery is stealing and hell. In his world, in order to 'do the right thing' he has to betray his friend. Twain's irony cuts deep here. Because it's when Huck is most moral that he regards himself as sinful. His decision to choose hell over Jim's return to slavery is a rejection not only of the notion that Miss Watson owns Jim, it is a rejection of whole sets of values. His moral progress is the recognition that he must rely upon the 'sound heart' of his own experience rather than the 'deformed conscience' of his society. (A phrase from one of Twain's 1895 notebooks that summarizes the novel's central problem.)

Also, Huck's choice is an expression of empathy instead of abstract principles. Huck can't make the leap to abolitionist philosophy by reason. He doesn't have any philosophy. All he has is memories. Of Jim crying over his daughter 'Lizabeth when he'd hit her not knowing she was deaf. Of Jim's joy at seeing Huck alive after the Grangerford feud. Of them arguing like a family over King Solomon and the French on the raft. Huck's ethics come from a collection of moments of shared humanity. Not principles.

Some critics are right to suggest that Tom Sawyer's conversion of Jim's already-liberated freedom into a game ruins Huck's development by the end of the novel. But it can't undo it. By choosing hell, Twain shows us that conscience isn't some pre-determined compass given to us by society. It's something we construct out of choices about loyalty, love. Huck's not going to grow up to be respectable. He's going to be good.

Between 1849 and the mid 1860s Harriet Tubman accomplished roughly 13 separate trips back into the slave-holding South. All of which were in direct violation of federal law. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made it a crime not only to be an escaped slave, but also to aid others in doing so. The law levied fines up to $1,000 and prison sentences for abetting. It refused accused escaped slaves the right to a jury trial and it required all of the average citizens in the north to participate in these captures on demand. Tubman's response to this law was to re-enter the very regions it sought to secure. She had escaped from slavery in Dorchester County, MD in 1849. 
 Harriet employed an approach to undermine the logic of the Act. She moved people northward at night-often during the winter (lower patrols, longer darkness)-with the aid of the North Star and the help of other people spread along what would become known as the Underground Railroad. Following 1850 the scope of the law extending into free states meant she could no longer use Philadelphia or even New York as final destinations. Thus Tubman expanded her routes to St. Catharines, Ontario, Canada. Where the British law ensured the escapees were protected from US marshals. She is said to have personally led around 70 enslaved individuals to freedom (including members of her own family) despite rumors of a $40,000 reward on her head for capture. 
 It's these repeated missions that made these efforts a direct challenge to the Fugitive Slave Act-as opposed to just escaping. Short answer: Yes, it's normal to have soreness at 6 weeks after ACL reconstruction. But it's important to consider *what kind* of soreness it is. 
 I'm 4 months out from hamstring graft ACL reconstruction (Feb 14th Johns Hopkins) and at 6 weeks still had daily aches/pain, particularly near the incision sites and along the inside of my knee from where they took out the hamstring tendon. My physical therapist said it's normal because the graft is at its most vulnerable point in terms of healing (so-called "ligamentization") at 6 weeks and likely you're starting to increase your activity. Walking more, maybe stationary bike, possibly doing leg presses. So you're stressing the tissue in new ways. 
 Normal at 6 weeks: 
 Achey/dull pain after PT, after being on your feet for extended periods of time. 
 Soreness near portal incisions and donor site. 
 Stiffness after sitting in one place for a while. 
 Some (slight) swelling which resolves overnight. 
 NOT normal and should call surgeon: 
 Sudden and sharp pain (particularly with pivot motions) 
 New and severe swelling which is not resolving with elevation and ice. 
 Redness/warmth/fever (potentially infection. Please don't delay!) 
 Knee instability/feeling as if knee is "giving out" 
 Calf pain (could be a clot!) 
 Surgeon told me general guideline is that it should be improving (generally) week-to-week even if it varies day to day. If you're seeing flat or increasing soreness over a 2-week period you should get it checked out. 
 Some things that helped me were icing for 15-20 min after PT each time. Continuing quad sets and heel slides even when sore (movement helps) and sleeping with a pillow under my knee. Also make sure you're not limping and compensating with your hip which can cause soreness that can be confused with knee pain. 
 But, I'm just some random internet person. Not your surgeon. Call them if something doesn't feel right. They'll probably have a nurse line and much rather deal with a "silly" question than have you ignore a potential complication. 6 weeks is pretty early. It can be 3-4 months before a lot of people feel really "good".

tl;dr The answer is yes, it's perfectly normal to be sore at 6 weeks after ACL reconstruction.  But what kind of soreness. 
 I'm 4 months post-hamstring ACL reconstruction (had surgery at Johns Hopkins on 2/14).  I had soreness every day (especially in incision areas and on the inside of my knee where they took out hamstring tendon) at 6 weeks.  My PT noted that this was normal.  The graft is in the weakest phase of the healing process (called "ligamentization") at 6 weeks.  And you're likely increasing your activity (walking more, stationary bike, maybe start doing leg presses) and so you're putting more stresses on the tissue. 
 NORMAL at 6 weeks would be: 
 Dull achy after physical therapy sessions or after long periods of being on your feet 
 Sore around incision portals/donor site area 
 Stiffness if you sit for long periods of time in a fixed position 
 Minor swelling that diminishes overnight 
 
 NOT NORMAL at 6 weeks and you should call your surgeon 
 Sharp/sudden pain, particularly with pivoting 
 Noticable increase in swelling that isn't responding to ice and elevation 
 Redness/warmth/fever (could be infection; don't put this off) 
 Knee instability or a feeling of "giving way" 
 Calf pain (could be blood clot) 
 
 My surgeon's guideline is that you should be seeing general improvement from week to week, even if day to day is more variable.  If you're not seeing any improvements or it's getting worse over 2 weeks, definitely call. 
 
 I found that icing 15-20 min after PT sessions every time was helpful.  I did quad sets and heel slides when I could (even if sore, getting some movement is good).  I put a pillow under my knee when I sleep.  Also, make sure you're not limping.  Using your hip to compensate can cause soreness that you confuse with the knee. 
 
 Again, I'm just a dude on the internet.  Not your surgeon.  If it doesn't feel right, call their office.  They have nurse lines for most places.  They'd rather you ask a "dumb" question and they figure something out than there be a complication.  You're still in the early days.  Most people don't feel "good" until 3-4 months.  It's early days for you at 6 weeks.

The key is oven (or better yet, toaster oven/air fryer) reheating. Microwave ruins the crust (it just makes it rubbery cardboard) because it's just cooking the water in the breading. 
 To reheat: 
 1. Let the chicken reach room temperature for 20-30 minutes. Cooking cold directly from the fridge will result in uneven cooking. You'll overcook the outside to try and warm up the center. 
 2. Preheat your oven to 400F (200C). 
 3. Use a wire rack and sheet pan. This is critical that most people miss. You want the air underneath it to keep the bottom from getting steamed and soggy. It will do this if you just put the pieces on the pan. 
 4. Cook bone-in for 15-20 minutes, boneless/tenders for 10-12 minutes. Flip halfway. You want an internal temp of 165F (74C). Use instant read thermometer on the thickest part (near bone if you have bone). 
 5. Do not use foil or cover it. That'll trap steam and ruin it. 
 If you have an air fryer, it'll be even faster and probably more crisp. 375F (190C) for 4-6 minutes. You don't need to flip. The air fryer moves air all around it. I've done leftover KFC style thighs and Popeye's tenders this way and they were still almost as crisp as new. 
 Also, if the crust still feels kinda soft after reheating, put it under your broiler for the last 60-90 seconds. Watch it carefully to not burn. The direct blast of heat helps make any remaining parts more crisp than what convection cooking achieved. 
 Do not reheat it in the microwave. Don't bother if you don't care about the crust at all. Even 30 seconds in the microwave will visibly soften it.

The oven or even better - the toaster oven/air fryer, never use the microwave! The microwave just heats up the water that gets trapped inside the breading, which turns the crust into rubbery cardboard. 
 So: 
 1. Let the chicken sit out to come up to room temp for 20-30 minutes or so before re-heating. Heating something cold and directly to hot (from the fridge) is a problem, you end up burning the outside a bit too much in order to heat up the inside. 
 2. Heat the oven up to 400F (200C). Place a wire rack on a sheet pan. This is the key step that people forget and is the most important. The hot air coming up from below prevents the bottom from steaming up and getting soggy. This is what happens if you put the pieces right on the pan. 
 3. Bake bone-in chicken for 15-20min.  Bake boneless or tenders for 10-12min. Flip over halfway.  Looking for an internal temperature of 165F (74C).  Use an instant read thermometer, checking near the thickest part (near bone). 
 4. No foil / no cover. It traps the steam, which is the opposite of what you're trying to do. 
 Air fryer is even quicker and arguably crisper. 375F (190C)  for 4-6 minutes. No need to flip over. It has air circulation from all sides. This has worked great for me with leftover KFC style thighs and Popeyes tenders. Both came out nearly as crispy as fresh. 
  You can try to do the last 60-90seconds under a broiler (watching carefully so it doesn't burn). If after re-heating the crust still seems a bit soft. The blast of hot air directly underneath helps to crisp up anything that convection missed.

Dense, clean toothpick banana bread is a classic sign of not baking enough and/or having too much moisture. The toothpick test fails in this case. The wetness from the bananas is extreme. Even when starches have set enough to prevent stickiness on a skewer, it's still possible to have a gummy, dense center. 
 Here's what I would look into: 
 1) Probably your oven temp is off. Get an oven thermometer (Target $8-ish). My old GE was 25°F cool so outsides set much earlier than inside. Almost always dense middles are because of this. 
 2) Internal temp better than toothpick. Banana bread done at 200-205°F in the middle. Use thermapen. Any instant read. Remove when 200°F. It'll carry over perfectly. 
 3) Probably you're using too much banana. Most recipes want around 1 cup mashed. That's maybe 3 medium bananas (240g?). If you're throwing in 5 large "cause they're going bad" then you've probably got an extra 1/2 cup of liquid or so in there. It won't bake out as the banana, it'll just bake as gumminess. Freeze the extras. 
 4) Look at leavening. Baking soda goes bad quickly. If it's been open since 2023, replace. Put it in hot water and see if it bubbles vigorously. Throw it away. 
 5) Bake at a lower temp for longer time. Try 325°F instead of 350°F for 60-75min. 9x5. Slower baking helps the inside catch up. Cover w/ foil after 45 min if it's browning too quickly. 
 6) Don't overmix. Just mix until flour is gone. Chewy, tight texture from gluten development. 
 7) Cool completely in pan (at least an hour). Warm banana bread will make middle feel denser and more wet than it actually is when slicing. 
 
 If I had to guess, fix this. Get the thermometer and bake to 200-205°F. That's how I finally fixed this exact problem (after 2yrs of dense bread) for me.

Dense banana bread, and a clean toothpick... that usually points to underbaking and too much moisture. Clean toothpick can be a bad indicator. Bananas make the batter really wet. The center can be super gummy and dense even if the starches have set and there's nothing on a skewer. Check these things: 
 1. I bet your oven is inaccurate. Buy an oven thermometer (like $8 at Target). My old GE oven was 25°F under. So my banana bread would crust over on the outside while the middle wouldn't quite get there. This is the number one cause of dense middles. 
 2. Don't rely on the toothpick. You want banana bread to reach an internal temp of 200-205°F in the middle. I use a Thermapen. Instant read temp any kind. Pull it at 200°F and let it fully carryover bake. 
 3. You might be adding too much banana. A lot of recipes call for ~1 cup of banana mash. 3 medium bananas, ~240g. If you're adding 5 big bananas b/c they're going bad... that's maybe an extra 1/2 cup liquid. It won't bake out any of the excess banana. It just means gummy. Freeze the extras. 
 4. Leavening check. Baking soda breaks down quickly. If you've had it open since 2023, probably replace it. Drop it in hot water. No vigorous fizzing? Replace. 
 5. Reduce oven temp, increase time. Try 325°F instead of 350°F for maybe 60-75 minutes. 9x5 pan. The longer slower baking helps the middle catch up to the edges. After 45 minutes tent it with foil if it's browning too fast. 
 6. Don't over mix. Just mix til the flour disappears. You don't want to develop gluten. It'll make it chewy and dense. 
 7. Let it cool all the way in the pan. (at least an hour) If you cut warm banana bread, it can seem like the middle is dense and extra moist. 
 
 I'd say the best fix is to get a thermometer and cook to 200-205°F. That fixed my issue of having dense banana bread after 2 years of banana bread.

This is due to the fact that numbers in javascript are stored as IEEE 754 doubles, and 0.1 and 0.2 are not exactly representable as binary. So they're stored as the best approximated value. 0.1 is actually stored as approximately 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827 and 0.2 is actually stored as approximately 0.200000000000000011102230246251565. So if you add these together and round to the closest representable double, you get 0.30000000000000004, which is not 0.3. This isn't specific to javascript. It's like that in python, java, C, and really anything that uses the standard floating point operations (as defined by IEEE 754). Go try it out in a Node.js console or your web browser dev tools by typing in "0.1 + 0.2" and you'll see it right there. 
 No, don't use raw floats for doing arithmetic with the intent of then comparing or adding up precisely. Here's some good ways to handle money: 
 1. Do all operations using integer cents/minor units. $19.99 would be stored as 1999 (as an int). Then do all your operations on integers. Just divide by 100 to display it. This is easiest solution and will work well unless you want to do things like use fractional cents, or really big totals. 
 2. Use decimal library. Like decimal.js, big.js, big.number.js. These libraries represent numbers as base-10 decimals instead of binary floats. So "0.1 + 0.2" will actually give you "0.3". So for example: new Decimal('0.1').plus('0.2').toString() returns "0.3" 
 3. Use the native BigInt to do math on whole-cent integers if you don't need to do decimal during any operations. (This is nice because bigints don't have floating point precision issues for big ints.) 
 4. If you're in a newer environment, also be aware of the upcoming Number.prototype.toFixed issues. Number.toFixed() doesn't actually solve the precision issue. It just takes the display string and rounds it. So you don't want to use toFixed() to actually calculate anything. You just use it to format things. 
 Floating point for measuring and graphics. Ints or decimal for money.

If you work for a qualifying nonprofit or government employer, make sure you're qualifying for PSLF before overpaying. 
 So, if you have $42k in federal direct loans and think you're going to get 120 payments in, then I'd argue most of the time you want to make the required income driven payments and then invest your extra cash rather than go pay off something that might be forgiven.  For qualifying payments and employment it matters (according to studentaid.gov) so don't count your chickens before they hatch on forgiveness.  Make sure you check your account and see what's up with your employer.

 With the loan you're guaranteed 6.8% return by paying it down.  With the Roth IRA you might make more with investments over the long haul (decades), but might also take some losses.  6.8% is not "cheap" debt...

Once the 2026 contribution time frame has passed, that's likely gone (or at least it can't be made up).  I mean, you can pay the loan extra next year, but you can't go back and make some 2026 Roth room that wasn't used.

If you're highly focused on being debt free or your emergency savings are low, then I'd prioritize loan after grabbing employer match.

Yup, it's fairly safe (this combo is actually a common well-studied one for mitigating migraines). Ibuprofen and acetominophen are different mechanisms (ibuprofen is an NSAID for reducing inflammation; acetaminophen is still not fully understood but more of a central action), so they don't "compete" for the same stuff and can be taken at once. 
 Common practice for typical adult w/ no contraindications is to take 400mg ibuprofen + 500-1000mg acetominophen at once when you start to get migraine symptoms. OTC combo products (eg Excedrin Migraine with 250mg acetominophen + 250mg aspirin plus 65mg caffeine) also use this "more than one mechanism" principle (although that's aspirin instead of ibuprofen). 
 Max daily dose of acetominophen is 3000-4000mg for healthy adult (a lot of clinicians recommend you shouldn't exceed 3000mg/day if you regularly take it). You're fine with a 500mg dose even if you take another one 6-8 hours later. 
 Max OTC daily dose of ibuprofen is usually 1200mg/day (400mg every 6 hours), but a doc can prescribe up to 3200mg/day for some people. 
 Be careful not to take a 3rd medication without checking their labels - many "migraine" or "sinus" combo pills already include acetominophen in them. So you may be taking 2 things containing it and could go over the daily max. 
 Anyone with liver problems or is a heavy drinker (for acetominophen) or with kidney problems or stomach ulcers or GERD or on blood thinners like warfarin (for ibuprofen). Also, if pregnant or over 65 or on other daily meds, check with pharmacist. This takes 2 minutes at the counter and they can let you know if there are any interactions specifically for your other medications. 
 If you're getting migraines enough that you're taking this combo more than 2-3 times/week, it's probably time to get a doc to do some preventative stuff for you instead of just taking OTC combos all the time (since taking things all the time can itself lead to medication overuse headache).

MEMORANDUM 
 To: Maria Kowalski, CEO. Jan Freitag, CTO From: Elena Rasmussen, Data Protection Officer Date: 12 May 2025 Re: GDPR Compliance on Data Retention for Kowalski Customer Database Expansion to EU

Purpose. As we prepare to roll out the Kowalski customer database to new EU territories (Germany, Netherlands, Poland) beginning 1 September 2025, this memo outlines our data retention requirements under the GDPR and steps needed prior to launch.

Summary of Requirements

1. Specified Retention Periods (Art. 5(1)(e)). Data must not be retained beyond the time needed. Existing practice of indefinite retention of inactive customer data is not compliant. Retention plan proposed: Transactional data: 7 years (Polish and German tax requirements). Marketing data/consent: Duration of consent + 3 years for audit trail. Browsing data (abandoned cart): Max 90 days.

2. Automation of Deletion. Automated deletion/anonymization processes need to be built into the CRM (Engineering, P. Nowak's team) by 15 August 2025. Quarterly manual deletions are not sufficient for expected 2.4M new EU records.

3. Minimize Data during Migration. Only data required for order fulfillment and compliance should be migrated. Must delete legacy data (e.g., ID scans used in 2016-2019 fraud screening) before migration, not after.

4. Records of Processing (Art. 30). Retention must be part of our processing register, subject to review by our supervisory authority (likely Polish UODO, since Warsaw will be lead entity for EU processing).

5. Data Subject Rights. Must update retention periods in privacy policies and when handling access/deletion requests. Certain data excluded (e.g., legal hold due to pending legal action w/ Bergmann Logistics). Need to track legal holds.

Risks. Incompliant data retention risks fines of up to ?20M or 4% global turnover. Weakens our basis for marketing (Art. 6(1)(a)).

Actions & Responsibility

Action Owner Deadline
Approve Retention Plan Executive Committee 30 May 2025
Delete old ID scans IT Ops (L. Hansen) 20 June 2025
Build deletion processes Engineering (P. Nowak) 15 Aug 2025
Revise Privacy/Art. 30 DPO office 22 Aug 2025

Need 30 minutes for finalizing retention plan during 28 May leadership meeting. €85K required for tools and external review (in FY2025 compliance budget).

Date: Sep 21, 2026
Subject: Summary of Q2 FY26 Financial Results

Q2 FY26 consolidated revenues totaled $412.6M representing a YoY growth of 7.1% vs. $385.2M in Q2 FY25, largely supported by strong Medical Devices (+11.4%) and Consumer Diagnostics (+9.2%). However, Pharma gross margin declined to 38.4% (down from 44.9% in Q2 FY25) due to 650bp decline in gross margin, thereby suppressing healthy top-line growth and contributing to consolidated operating margin decline to 19.8% from 22.3%.

The pharma gross margin decline is driven by three factors:

(1) The active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) costs from our Hyderabad/Cork facilities increased 14% due to supply chain issues in March/April

(2) Loss of patent protection on our second-highest revenue branded drug, Nexovant, since January has resulted in earlier-than-forecast generic substitution, which resulted in a ~18% decline in average selling price in the US market

(3) We had one-time inventory write-downs ($6.2M) in May related to the discontinued lots at Raleigh manufacturing site

With pharma revenue essentially flat at $148.3M (YoY growth of +0.6%), Pharma is disproportionately weighing on the overall cost base without matching corresponding revenue lift. Our forecast on full-year pharma GM would likely bottom out at ~39% (down ~500bps from FY25 at 44.1%) if trends persist.

We recommend the following actions for Q3: (1) accelerate the API dual-sourcing effort from our Basel supplier to stabilize input costs by YE. (2) expedite the reformulation effort of Nexovant-XR and aim for FDA submission by 11/15 to partially recapture branded pricing. (3) Complete the process audit at Raleigh site by 10/10 to avoid similar write-down scenarios in the future.

We will provide a detailed pharma margin recovery plan to the Board at the Oct 14th meeting.

 Corporate & Shared Services - 98% outstanding 6
 Retail Banking Operations - 96% outstanding 41
 Commercial Lending - 93% outstanding 22
 Wealth Management - 89% outstanding 38
 International (Singapore & London offices) 91% outstanding 12

NOTE: Within Wealth Management (63 licensed relationship managers) they have 100% completion of the enhanced KYC training. There is an issue with support staff.

Findings
 The major reasons for not completing are: (1) either on extended leave medical or parental leave (27) or (2) Q2 new hires delayed (44). Total with no apparent reason 48. The delay in Singapore office related to a schedule issue with our system migration in May. Held make-up classes June 3-5.

Remediation Plan
 1. June 16 - 20. Direct supervisor of 48 (unexplained) outstanding employees will be sending them a written notice. Individuals are enrolled in mandatory live session on June 24 and July 8.
 2. June 30 - Auto enroll for training all returning to work individuals from leave within 5 business days of their return. (HR will check this through their payroll re-activation flags.)
 3. July 15 - All Q2 new hires will complete the onboarding training. (We have made this a requirement for probationary review period.)
 4. July 31. Any remaining outstanding individuals will be reported up to the various divisional heads. Under the Section 4.3 of our AML policy they will be removed from customer facing systems.
 5. August 5. Final report for attestation to Board Audit & Risk Committee.

Regulatory
 Our regulator expects all our staff to participate in annual refresher training related to AML. Last years' examination indicated our 91% completion rate was acceptable but suggested we needed to put procedures in place to "push" on the laggards. That is part of what is being put in place in this plan.

Budget Impact
 The expense for remediation estimated $18.5K (live session facilitation and LMS licensing). This will be within our current compliance training budget of $420K for FY2025.

No additional actions from leadership are being requested at this time. Next status update to be provided on August 5.

paper_section_00_glm.text:
Abstract
The hepatic uptake transporter, OATP1B1 (SLCO1B1) is responsible for the hepatic uptake of many endogenous substrates and clinically relevant drugs such as statins. Genetic variation in SLCO1B1, including common loss of function alleles (e.g. rs4149056 T>C polymorphism, c.521T>C, Val174Ala) is linked to elevated statin systemic exposure, which is associated with an increased risk of myopathy. However, a more precise understanding of the magnitude of contribution of OATP1B1 to overall hepatocellular uptake for individual substrates is lacking. In this study, we sought to directly measure the contribution of OATP1B1 to hepatic uptake by establishing a CRISPR-Cas9 mediated SLCO1B1 knockout in HepG2 cells. By using two single guide RNAs (targeting SLCO1B1 exons 2 and 6) we were able to generate confirmed clonal SLCO1B1 knockout cells (verified by Sanger sequencing, RT-qPCR showing >95% decrease in SLCO1B1 transcript levels and Western blot showing lack of OATP1B1 protein). Whole genome off-target evaluation was done by targeted amplicon sequencing on the top 10 predicted off-target sites, with no indels detected at an allele frequency greater than 1.2%. Hepatic uptake experiments using fluorescently labeled pravastatin (10µM) were conducted at 37°C for 5 min, revealing that pravastatin uptake was 43.0% ± 3.8% (mean ± SEM, n=4 independent experiments, p<0.001, two-tailed unpaired t-test) lower in knockout clones compared to wild-type HepG2 cells and non-targeting guide RNA. This remaining uptake was refractory to the OATP inhibitor rifampicin (100 µM) but was partially blocked by probenecid, indicating that additional organic anion transport pathways (likely OATP1B3 and Na+-Taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide) were also involved (both of which were still expressed in the knockout clones). Kinetic studies suggested that the decrease in uptake observed was due to a 46% decrease in maximal transport capacity (Vmax: 285 ± 31 vs. 528 ± 44 pmol/mg protein/5 min) with no significant effect on apparent Km. This work provides a direct measure of the magnitude of OATP1B1 contribution to statin uptake in a human hepatocyte model and a validated isogenic knockout system for screening of substrate-and genotype-dependent drug disposition, which may have implications for precision dosing of OATP1B1 substrates in loss of function allele carriers.

Abstract
The hepatic uptake transporter encoded by the solute carrier organic anion transporter family 1B member 1 (OATP1B1, SLCO1B1) is responsible for the uptake of many endogenous compounds and clinically relevant drugs such as statins, into hepatocytes. Although common loss-of-function variants in SLCO1B1, like the single nucleotide polymorphism rs4149056 T>C (c.521T>C, Val174Ala) are linked to higher systemic exposure to statins and an increased risk of developing myopathy, the quantitative contribution of OATP1B1 on the overall hepatocellular uptake of specific substrates is not fully understood. We employed CRISPR-Cas9-based SLCO1B1 knockout in HepG2 cells to directly determine the transporter's role in hepatic uptake. With two single guide RNAs against exons 2 and 6 of SLCO1B1 we generated clonal knockout cell lines that were validated by Sanger sequencing, RT-qPCR (>95% decrease in transcript levels of SLCO1B1) and Western blot (no OATP1B1 protein present). Targeted amplicon sequencing of the ten most predicted off-target loci showed no indels with more than 1.2% allele frequency in whole genome off-target analysis. Uptake studies at 37°C for 5 min with fluorescent labeled pravastatin (10 µM) showed a 43.0% ± 3.8% (mean ± SEM, n = 4 independent experiments, p < 0.001, two-tailed unpaired t-test) decrease of uptake in SLCO1B1 knockout clones compared to wild-type HepG2 cells and non-targeting guide RNA controls. Remaining uptake was not inhibited by the OATP inhibitor rifampicin (100 µM) but was partially inhibited by probenecid. This suggests involvement of other organic anion transport systems, most likely including OATP1B3 and Na + -taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide, both of which were expressed in the knockout clones. Kinetic characterization showed that the decrease in uptake was caused by a 46% decrease in the maximal transport capacity (Vmax; 285 ± 31 vs. 528 ± 44 pmol/mg protein/5 min) without significant changes in apparent Km. This directly quantifies the contribution of OATP1B1 to statin uptake in the human hepatocyte model and provides a validated isogenic knockout platform to screen genotype and substrate specific drug disposition. It has potential to enable precision dosing of OATP1B1 substrates in loss-of-function allele carriers.

Methods
A sample of 240 veterans (M age = 47.3 y, SD = 12.1 y, 68% male) were enrolled from March 2021 through November 2022 in outpatient clinics at VA Puget Sound Health Care System (Seattle, WA) and VA Boston Healthcare System (Boston, MA). Criteria included diagnosis of DSM-5 chronic insomnia disorder, Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) score ≥15, and lack of active suicidal ideation or untreated psychosis. Comorbid PTSD veterans (n = 142, 59%) were included to match the intended population. Of the 412 referrals screened, 240 were randomized 1:1 with a computer-generated permuted block design (block size 4, site and PTSD-stratified). Veterans were assigned to cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) (n = 120) or an active control condition consisting of sleep hygiene education and attention-matched contact (n = 120).
The CBT-I intervention comprised 6 weekly 50 min individual sessions administered by 14 doctoral level psychologists, who were trained to fidelity criterion ≥90% on standardized checklist. Components consisted of sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, and relapse prevention. Control condition participants received 1 session (30 min) of sleep hygiene education, followed by 5 weekly 20-min check-in phone calls. Veterans were evaluated at baseline, post-treatment (week 7), and 6 months follow-up (to May 2023). The primary outcome measure was the ISI score. Secondary outcomes included sleep efficiency from sleep diaries, 7 consecutive nights of actigraphy (Actiwatch-2), scores on the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5), and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Outcome assessors were blinded to condition. The study was powered to a sample of n = 120 per arm to detect between-group differences of 4 points on ISI (SD = 6.5), with 15% attrition, and α = .05 (2-tailed). Primary data analyses used intention-to-treat linear mixed effects models with random participant and site intercepts. Models controlled for baseline ISI and PTSD status.
The protocol was approved by VA Central Institutional Review Board (IRB #2020-0847). It was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04739228). All participants gave written informed consent prior to randomization.

METHODS
Study participants included 240 veterans (mean age = 47.3 years, SD = 12.1; 68% male), screened from March 2021 to November 2022 in the outpatient clinic settings of the VA Puget Sound Health Care System (Seattle, WA) and VA Boston Healthcare System (Boston, MA). Inclusion criteria included DSM-5 chronic insomnia disorder and Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) scores ≥15; absence of active suicidal ideation and untreated psychosis. Veterans with PTSD (n = 142, 59%) were included to represent target population. From 412 referrals, 240 were randomized (1:1) using computer-generated permuted block randomization (4 block size, stratified by site, PTSD status) to either cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for insomnia (n = 120) or active control condition of sleep hygiene education + attention-matched contact (n = 120).

CBT-I consisted of 6 weekly individual (50 min) sessions by 14 doctoral psychologists (trained to ≥90% of fidelity using standardized checklist) comprising sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring and relapse prevention strategies. Control condition included 1 (30 min) sleep hygiene session + 5 weekly (20 min) check-in phone calls. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, post-treatment (7 weeks) and 6-month follow-up (May 2023). Primary outcome was ISI. Secondary outcomes were: sleep efficiency from sleep diary; 7-night actigraphy (Actiwatch2); PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5); Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9). Blinded outcome assessment. Sample size of n = 120/group had 0.90 power to detect 4-point difference (SD = 6.5) between groups on ISI, assuming 15% attrition (α = .05, 2-tailed). Intention-to-treat analysis was performed using linear mixed effects models (with random participant and site intercept, adjusting for baseline ISI, PTSD status). Protocol was approved by VA Central Institutional Review Board (IRB#2020-0847) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04739228). Written informed consent was obtained from participants before randomization.

paper_section_04_luna.text:
A large study from 2015 (Open Science Collaboration) is highly suggestive that the published literature for psychology is less reliable than it appears. However, its findings do not imply that the original studies were mostly false. The Open Science Collaboration tried to replicate 100 studies from 2008 that were published in *Psychological Science*, *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, and *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition*. While statistically significant results were obtained for 97% of the original studies, only 36% of the replication studies yielded statistically significant results. Furthermore, replication effect sizes averaged around half the size of the original effect (r = .197 vs. r = .403), suggesting that failure of replications is often not due to the phenomenon being completely absent, but rather to a large overestimate of the true size. [Open Science Collaboration, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac4716)

Many methodological/institutional reasons could account for the difference between original and replication findings. In particular, publication bias leads to a disproportionate number of surprising statistically significant results. Also, data analysis flexibility and small samples can lead to highly variable estimates that are unlikely to be replicable. Finally, the original studies may have relied on some unique cultural settings, samples, experimenter expectations, procedures, etc., that are difficult to perfectly replicate. In other words, a failure of direct replication may be due to boundary conditions and differences in methodology, not just fraud or entirely wrong theories. Indeed, 47% of the original effect sizes were in the 95% confidence interval of the replication study, and 39% of the findings were considered replicated by the replication teams.

But the difference between original and replication findings make it clear that statistical significance is not an adequate proxy for scientific reliability. The big, preregistered collaborative nature of the study helped move the conversation towards power, effect size estimation, openness, accumulation of evidence. In that sense, the most important impact of this study was not to provide one estimate for the true replication rate of psychology, but to illustrate empirically how our current research practices can systematically bias our beliefs in the published research. More reproducibility can be achieved with preregistration, larger samples, openness (data and materials), registered reports, and increased acceptance of null results.

In 2015, the Open Science Collaboration showed that published psychology was not as reliable as the literature implied. This does not mean that most original studies were bogus, though. The Open Science Collaboration tried to reproduce 100 studies that appeared in 2008 in *Psychological Science*, *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* and *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition*. Even though 97% of the original studies produced statistically significant results, only 36% of the replications were statistically significant. The effect sizes in the replications were also on average about half as big as in the originals (r = .197 compared to r = .403), which means that often the replication failure was due to a substantial overestimate and not due to the nonexistence of the phenomenon. [Open Science Collaboration, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac4716)

A combination of methodological and institutional reasons might explain this difference. In particular, surprising statistically significant results are more likely to be published, while flexible analyses and low sample sizes can lead to unstable results that are not reproducible. Also, original studies may rely on certain cultural conditions, sample characteristics, experimenter expectations or procedural details that are not easily replicated. Therefore, failing a direct replication does not necessarily mean fraudulent behavior or fundamentally misguided theory, but may be due to boundary conditions or methodological issues. In line with this, 47% of the effect sizes in the original studies were contained in the 95% confidence interval of the replication study and 39% of the results were considered to be replicated by the replication teams.

Still, the difference between original and replication shows that the criterion for scientific validity cannot simply be whether a result was statistically significant. The large scale, preregistered, collaborative nature of this study directed attention to issues such as power, effect size estimation, transparency and cumulative evidence. Therefore, the real value of the study is not so much a single estimate of the "true" psychology replication rate, but the empirical evidence of how research practices can systematically increase confidence in the published results. To increase reproducibility, we need preregistration, large sample sizes, open data and materials, registered reports, and an openness to publication of null results.

paper_section_06_glm.text:
1. Introduction
The Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) began a run of unorthodox policy rate cuts in September 2021 that would shape the most important monetary policy experiment of the recent period. In about four months, the CBRT cut the policy rate from 19% to 14% despite a year-on-year consumer price inflation close to 20%. The trend continued in 2022 and 2023, and the policy rate was eventually reduced to as low as 8.5% by February 2023 even as the headline inflation accelerated to over 80% in October 2022, the highest inflation rate in Türkiye's republican history. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan repeatedly explained and the government's economic program presented in December 2021 enshrined the intellectual underpinning of this policy stance which is the belief that high interest rates cause inflation, the complete reverse of the standard monetary theory. This view was dubbed in the Turkish public as " faiz sebep, enflasyon sonuç" (cause-interest, result-inflation).

The policy episode is interesting in that it provides a natural experiment for the actions of a large economy integrated to the global financial markets as it actively pursued a policy stance that was the complete opposite of the inflation targeting consensus just when the global economy was facing the post-pandemic surge in demand and the commodity price shock after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 which were pushing the inflation rates up globally. The major challenge in this paper will be to separate the global effects from domestic policy effects.

The paper is the contribution of the literature in three dimensions: 1) we provide a monthly dataset on CBRT policy actions, Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) price indices, credit default swaps for sovereign debt, and USD/TRY exchange rate changes between January 2010 and December 2023 to explain the timing and transmission of the unorthodox policy easing cycle. 2) We estimate the counterfactual inflation without the policy rate cuts using a structural vector autoregression approach, as well as the synthetic control approach where the policy period is compared to the weighted average of other emerging economies (including Brazil, South Africa, and Poland). 3) We also provide the behavioral analysis where we use TÜİK consumer expectations surveys and CBRT surveys of market participants to demonstrate the gradual unanchoring of the inflation expectations, as 12-months-ahead inflation expectation increases over 60% by mid-2022.

Our results are relevant for the discussion on the costs of abandoning the institutional monetary policy frameworks, on the pass-through of exchange rate in highly dollarized economies, as well as the political economy of central bank independence. The Turkish episode that ended with the adoption of orthodox policies by Governor Hafize Gaye Erkan in June 2023 with a 6-month increase of policy rates from 8.5% to 40% provides an important natural experiment that should not be neglected for Türkiye or beyond.

Introduction In September 2021, the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) embarked on an unorthodox series of monetary policy rate cuts that would lay the foundation for one of the most important monetary policy episodes in modern history. In the space of four months, policy rate was lowered from 19% to 14% when headline consumer price inflation was already approaching 20% on an annual basis. The path of rate cuts extended throughout 2022 and 2023, until the policy rate reached a low of 8.5% in February 2023, even though headline inflation reached above 80% in October 2022, the highest level ever recorded in the republican history of Türkiye. The intellectual underpinning of this policy stance, repeatedly voiced by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and as part of the economic program announced in December 2021, was the belief that high interest rates are inflationary in nature (a reversal of conventional monetary economics) that later became popular in the Turkish discourse as ' faiz sebep, enflasyon sonuç ' (interest is the cause, inflation is the result).

We are witnessing a unique natural experiment in the sense that a large open economy chose to explicitly adopt a monetary policy stance that was exactly the opposite of the inflation targeting consensus at a time when global events (postpandemic demand recovery and commodity price shock due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022) were already driving up global inflation. Isolating the impact of policy decisions from these global factors is the main empirical challenge of our paper.

We provide three contributions to the literature. First, we gather a monthly dataset from January 2010 to December 2023, encompassing the decisions made by the CBRT, Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) price indexes, credit default swaps (CDS) of the sovereign and USD/TRY exchange rate changes to describe the evolution and transmission of the unorthodox easing period. Second, using a structural VAR framework and in conjunction with a synthetic control exercise relative to a weighted set of emerging market countries (Brazil, South Africa, Poland, etc.), we assess the counterfactual inflation outcomes in the absence of rate cuts. Third, we focus on behavioral aspects of the period. We present survey results obtained from the consumer expectation surveys of TÜİK and polls of market participants conducted by the CBRT to illustrate the gradual disanchoring of inflation expectations. Indeed, 12-month-ahead inflation expectations reach above 60% by mid-2022.

Our results are relevant to current discussions on the negative effects of dropping institutional monetary policy frameworks, pass-through of exchange rates in highly dollarized countries and political economy of central bank independence. The Turkish case culminating with the return to an orthodox policy stance with the appointment of Governor Hafize Gaye Erkan in June 2023 (increasing rates from 8.5% to 40% over a period of 6 months) is a cautionary natural experiment with implications far beyond the borders of Türkiye.

Results

The tensile properties were investigated for Ti-6Al-4V specimens produced by LPBF (laser power bed fusion) process for laser powers of 150 W, 175 W, 200 W, 225 W, and 250 W on the EOS M290 system. Scan speed (1200 mm/s), hatch distance (0.10 mm), and layer thickness (30 μm) were kept constant. Tensile testing was conducted for 10 dog bone (ASTM E8 subsize) specimens for each laser power after stress relief at 650 • C for 3 h in argon atmosphere. The specimens were fractured on an Instron 5985 machine at 1 mm/min crosshead speed.

As laser power increases from 150 W to 200 W, the ultimate tensile strength (UTS) increases from 1021 ± 18 MPa to maximum 1147 ± 12 MPa, and then decreases with laser powers of 225 W (1089 ± 24 MPa) and 250 W (1043 ± 31 MPa). The results are expressed as a mean value and standard deviation (n = 10). The effect of laser power on UTS is significant by a one-way ANOVA (F(4,45) = 26.7, p < 0.001). The post hoc analysis (Tukey HSD) identifies the 200 W group as significantly different compared to other laser power groups (p < 0.01) except for the 225 W group (p = 0.08). Similarly, yield strength reaches the maximum value (1068 ± 15 MPa) at 200 W laser power compared to 948 ± 21 MPa at 150 W laser power. The maximum elongation at fracture is measured at 200 W laser power (11.4 ± 0.9%) and minimum elongation at fracture (6.2 ± 1.3%) is measured at 250 W laser power. It is associated with increased porosity of 0.8% and 2.9% by micro-CT for 200 W and 250 W laser powers, respectively. It is due to instability of the keyhole mode of laser melting at higher energy density.

SEM (Zeiss Sigma 300) analysis of fracture surfaces at 250 W laser power shows spherical pores (30-80 μm diameter) associated with the keyhole mode. The pores are located primarily in the vicinity of the crack initiation point and correlate with lower ductility in the sample. For the case of 150 W laser power, the lack of fusion defects with irregular shape are present which correlate with lower UTS values. Total porosity is similar for both laser powers (1.1%). These results suggest the laser power of 200 W is the most favorable within the investigated range in this study for the given scan parameters to reach the best compromise between strength and ductility.

Results

Tensile behavior of laser powder bed fused (LPBF) Ti-6Al-4V samples was investigated for 5 laser power values (150 W, 175 W, 200 W, 225 W, 250 W) on EOS M290 printer at a fixed scan speed (1200 mm/s), hatch (0.10 mm) and layer thickness (30 µm). 10 dog bone (ASTM E8 subsize) samples were printed at each laser power. They were stress-relieved for 3 h at 650 °C (Ar atmosphere) and tested to failure on an Instron 5985 (crosshead speed 1 mm/min).

The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) was found to increase from 1021±18 MPa (150 W) to maximum value (1147±12 MPa at 200 W) then reduce to 1089±24 MPa (225 W) and 1043±31 MPa (250 W) (mean ± SD, n = 10). A one-way ANOVA test showed laser power to have a significant influence on UTS (F(4, 45) = 26.7, p < 0.001). Tukey HSD post-hoc analysis indicated significant differences between 200 W and other groups (p < 0.01) except 225 W (p = 0.08). Same trend was observed for yield strength (maximum at 200 W 1068±15 MPa vs 948±21 MPa at 150 W). Elongation at break was maximum at 200 W (11.4±0.9%) and decreased abruptly at 250 W (6.2±1.3%). This corresponded to a higher porosity value (0.8% vs 2.9% micro-CT) due to keyhole instability in higher energy density regime.

SEM (Zeiss Sigma 300) examination of fractographic features of 250 W samples showed round (keyhole) pores (diameter 30-80 µm), especially in the vicinity of the initiation of fracture, which is in agreement with the reduction in ductility. On the other hand, lack of fusion features (irregular geometry) were identified in 150 W sample which could explain their lower UTS with similar level of porosity (1.1%). This suggested 200 W to be the most suitable power in the selected range for a maximum strength-ductility compromise in the tested samples with fixed scan parameters as described here.

paper_section_10_luna.text:
Impacts of the BC carbon tax on greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing plants (2019 policy).

We study the impacts of British Columbia's carbon tax on greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing plants, with the 2019 policy setting as the focus of analysis. Although BC has a carbon tax since 2008, the BC carbon tax is raised to C$40 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent in April 2019, creating a large price signal on fossil fuel use. Confidential plant-level data on fuel spending, emissions, output and employment are utilized to build a panel of manufacturing emissions. We estimate an augmented difference in differences model that exploits the differential exposure to the carbon tax from different plants. Comparison is made between more carbon-intensive plants and less exposed plants. Plant and year fixed effects, sector trends and general economic trends are all taken into consideration.

The estimated impact of the carbon tax on manufacturing plant greenhouse gas emissions is about 4% less than counterfactual emission levels. A major contributor to the decrease in emissions is a drop in emission intensity. Emission intensity is about 6% lower. There is also a rise in output. Output is about 1.8% higher. These results suggest that the carbon tax did not just induce contraction of manufacturing activities, or closing plants, to lower emissions. There seems to be a shift in firms' production strategies, where more output is generated with less use of fossil fuel energy. This may reflect that investments in energy efficiency or productivity-improving technologies are made. The revenue-neutral nature of the carbon tax (tax revenue recycled through cuts to corporate income tax and other means) may have made it easier for firms to make abatement investments.

We find that there is measurable emissions reduction in manufacturing under BC's carbon pricing regime without contraction in aggregate plant output. Note however that our estimated impacts should not be interpreted as an identification of the independent impact of a new tax, introduced in 2019. The carbon tax was initiated in 2008 and the 2019 carbon tax rate is an escalation of an existing program.

British Columbia carbon tax and greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing plants: Evidence for 2019

We analyze the impact of British Columbia's carbon tax on the greenhouse gas emissions of manufacturing plants for 2019 policy settings. Despite the implementation of British Columbia's revenue-neutral carbon tax in 2008, its carbon tax rate, which imposes a significant price signal on the use of fossil fuels, escalated to C$40 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent in April 2019 for the provincial rate. We create a manufacturing greenhouse gas emissions panel, using confidential plant-level data on fuel costs, emissions, output, and employment. We estimate augmented difference-in-differences specifications that leverage the heterogeneity in plant exposure to the tax, comparing more carbon-intensive facilities to less exposed plants, adjusting for plant and year fixed effects, industry-wide patterns, and general economic conditions.

We find that greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing plants have decreased by around 4% relative to counterfactual values due to the introduction of the carbon tax. This impact is driven mainly by a 6% decrease in the emissions intensity with an increase of 1.8% in the output of the plant. Our results imply that this was not a pure contraction in manufacturing emissions or plant closures due to the policy. Rather, the policy likely enabled firms to enhance production output with reduced use of fossil-fuel-based energy, possibly by encouraging energy efficiency improvements and productivity-enhancing technologies. In this context, the revenue-neutral policy mechanism (recycling revenues from the carbon tax through lower corporate income taxes and other means) may have eased the cost of abating investments.

Our evidence implies that, for the manufacturing sector, the implementation of the carbon pricing regime in British Columbia led to measurable emissions reductions without negative consequences for overall plant output. Yet we caution that the estimated impacts cannot be taken as the impact of a new (2019) tax, as the policy was already in place since 2008, and the 2019 rate was an escalation of the existing policy.

paper_section_12_glm.text:
METHODS

IN SITU TEM ASSEMBLY OF OPEN CELL

The open-cell in situ TEM was performed on a FEI Titan 80-300 environmental TEM at 300 kV equipped with a Gatan OneView camera for continuous imaging at 25 fps. The growth of lithium dendrites was monitored in a nanoscale electrochemical cell assembled in a Hummingbird Scientific electrical biasing TEM holder. A half-cell configuration was employed, with a ~100 nm thick Li 2 O-coated lithium metal electrode obtained by scratching the metallic lithium foil (99.9% SigmaAldrich) using a W wire to utilize native Li 2 O as the solid electrolyte layer. The counter electrode used in this study was an electrochemically sharp copper wire (99.99% Alfa Aesar, 250 μm diameter) which was placed on the Li 2 O using piezoerically controlled manipulation with sub-10 nm precision.

ELECTROCHEMICAL METHODS

Keithley 2400 SourceMeter was used for galvanostatic charging through connection to the holder. Charging current was adjusted to provide an effective 1 C nanoscale contact current (10-50 A/cm 2 at electrode-electrolyte interface), measured at the nanoscale contact area. Current density was estimated based on the measured contact area of 0.01-0.05 μm 2 observed in TEM images. In parallel with charging, we applied a −2 V constant bias for nucleation facilitation in accordance with previous open cell set-ups.

TEM IMAGING

Bright-field imaging of the dendrite growth was done at 28,000-115,000× magnification. To mitigate beaminduced effects, the total electron dose was kept below 50 e -/Å 2 /s. Blanked beam control experiments were conducted to verify that electron irradiation does not influence dendrite morphology. The length of dendrite growth cycles was set to 60-180 s. For ensuring reproducibility, at least 12 independent cells were imaged in 3 experimental sessions (March-May 2024).

DATA ANALYSIS

Propagation velocity of the dendrite was determined by frame-by-frame growth front tracking using ImageJ (v1.54k). Kymograph analysis showed 5-40 nm/s velocity. The dendrite tip structure was determined with selected area electron diffraction, showing single crystal Li (bodycentered cubic structure) along the ⟨111⟩ growth direction. Mean ± std. dev. of cells is used for presenting quantitative results.

Methods

In situ TEM cell assembly
In situ TEM of open cell was performed with a FEI Titan 80-300 environmental TEM operating at 300 kV using Gatan OneView camera for continuous imaging (frame rate 25 fps). We studied lithium dendrite formation within a nanoscale electrochemical cell assembled in situ in the Hummingbird Scientific electrical biasing TEM holder. We utilized half cell geometry and formed a ~100 nm thick Li 2 O-coated lithium metal electrode by scratching metallic Li (99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) foil with tungsten wire. Therefore, we used native Li 2 O as solid electrolyte layer. As counter electrode we used sharp, electrochemically polished copper wire (99.99%, Alfa Aesar; d = 250 μm) which was in contact with the Li 2 O surface via piezoerically controlled manipulation with a sub-10 nm positioning accuracy.

Electrochemical protocol
We used a Keithley 2400 SourceMeter which was interfaced with the holder. We performed galvanostatic charging and calibrated charging currents for the effective nanoscale contact area to be 1 C rate, i.e., current density at the electrode-electrolyte interface in the range of 10-50 A/cm 2. The current density was estimated based on the contact area determined from TEM images (0.01-0.05 μm 2). In addition, we applied constant -2 V bias to facilitate the nucleation. This is in line with the previously reported open cell arrangements.

Imaging parameters
We recorded the dendrite growth in bright field at the magnification range of 28,000-115,000× with the total electron dose below 50 e -/Å 2 /s to reduce beam-induced effects. We have performed the control measurements with blanked electron beam and confirmed that the morphology of the dendrites is not affected by the electron beam. We recorded 60-180 s of each deposition cycle. We imaged at least twelve independent cells in each case and we reproduced the measurements on three different days (March-May 2024) to confirm reproducibility.

Data analysis
We calculated the velocity of the dendrite propagation based on frame-by-frame tracking of the growth front using ImageJ (v1.54k) software. We used kymograph analysis to obtain the velocities in the range of 5-40 nm/s. We investigated the structural characteristics of the dendrite tips with the help of selected area electron diffraction. We confirmed that the dendrite tips have a single crystalline Li with body centered cubic structure. The growth direction is ⟨111⟩. We show quantitative data in the form of mean ± standard deviation over all cells.

paper_section_14_sonnet.text:
Limitations

We discuss some of the limitations of our FL approach that we experienced across 12 hospitals. Firstly, we note that non-IID data across hospitals remained a challenge despite incorporating FedProx (μ=0.01) instead of vanilla FedAvg. The prevalence of pathology classes presented substantial variation in class imbalance from one site to another (for example, we had less than 40 positive pneumothorax cases from Site 7 -pediatric in Lyon- over 14 months of data collection versus more than 2100 cases from Site 3 -level 1 trauma center in Houston-), likely explaining the 6.8 difference in AUCs between the top and lowest performance site on held-out local test sets (0.91 vs. 0.843). Secondly, our harmonization preprocessing was not enough to fully deal with heterogeneity in scanner/acquisition (5 of the 12 hospitals were on GE Revolution CT scanners, whereas others were on a combination of Siemens SOMATOM/Canon Aquilion CT scanners) as there is likely lingering domain shift in reconstruction kernel and slice thickness that our histogram matching was not able to fully account for. Thirdly, our communication assumed all 12 sites had robust connectivity and synchronous 48h intervals between rounds over 9 months of training (Jan-Sep 2025), whereas 3 of the sites had dropout in at least one of the rounds and we had to resort to stale-client averaging which may have added a layer of bias towards intermittent infrastructure sites. Fourthly, despite not sharing raw imaging data, gradient sharing was performed without formal differential privacy considerations thus there is a potential risk for membership-inference attacks and/or gradient-inversion attacks, as pointed out by 2 of the IRBs involved (Houston & Lyon) but not fully addressed in the scope of the current study. Lastly, we used held-out test sets at each site instead of a completely external cohort. As such, our results have yet to be tested on any hospitals outside of the current consortium of 12 sites. We believe that incorporating personalized FL (eg cluster/site-specific adapters) and formal privacy considerations should be taken into account in future work before we consider deployment for any clinical applications.

Limitations

We discuss some limitations of our federated learning approach on the 12 participating hospital data. First, our approach is still somewhat limited by the non-IID data distribution of sites despite leveraging FedProx (μ=0.01) instead of vanilla FedAvg. For example, pathology class imbalance (i.e., prevalence) differed significantly from one site to another. Site 7, the pediatric hospital located in Lyon, only had <40 positive cases of pneumothorax in the 14 months of data collection, whereas Site 3 (level-1 trauma center located in Houston) had over 2100+ positive cases, which might explain the 6.8 AUC point differences between best and worst sites (0.91 vs 0.843 AUC, held-out local test set). Second, harmonization preprocessing did not completely handle the scanner and data acquisition heterogeneity between sites. 5 out of the 12 hospitals used GE Revolution CT scanners while the other sites had a mix of Siemens SOMATOM and Canon Aquilion. We likely still see a residual domain shift of reconstruction kernel and slice thickness despite our histogram matching approach. Third, our communication scheme requires stable communication and 48 hours synchronous FL round for all 12 sites during the 9-month (Jan-Sep 2025) training period. 3 sites at least had dropout for one round during the training period so we had to resort to the stale client averaging approach which might add another bias against sites with potential sporadic network infrastructure. Fourth, while we do not transmit raw imaging data between sites, gradient exchange does not have a formally established differential privacy, which might lead to potential exposure to membership inference/gradient inversion attacks (two participating IRBs in Houston and Lyon raised this issue but it is not fully within our scope to address in this study). Finally, since our evaluation is performed on site specific held-out test set, generalizability to other hospitals beyond this 12-site consortium has not yet been assessed. Future work needs to add personalized federated learning (e.g., cluster/site adapters) and privacy accounting approaches to address some of these limitations before we can think of actual clinical adoption.

Following the launch of the Chromium Single Cell Controller in Pleasanton, California by 10x Genomics on October 18, 2016, the field of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has evolved rapidly. The Chromium system, which combines the power of microfluidic droplets, gel beads with barcodes and unique molecular identifiers, allowed researchers to scale single-cell profiling by thousands of cells simultaneously, enabling a major leap in throughput and a reduction in costs and effort compared to previous plate-based protocols like Smart-seq2. This advancement in technology coincided with the launch of the Human Cell Atlas initiative in London at the Wellcome Trust on October 13-14, 2016, a large-scale effort to characterize the types and states of cells in humans across tissues. [10x Genomics](https://s28.q4cdn.com/592666581/files/doc_news/2016/10/18/10x-genomics-announces-new-low-cost-single-cell-instrument.pdf) [Human Cell Atlas](https://www.humancellatlas.org/event/human-cell-atlas-launch-meeting/)

In the years following, scRNA-seq has grown in throughput and biological coverage. New droplet technologies and sequencing/computational methods have made it possible to profile hundreds of thousands to millions of cells. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing has made it possible to profile tissues in frozen samples or archives, or those with challenging architecture and dissociation. Concurrently, there have been major advances in coupling transcriptome profiling with other types of molecular data, such as chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, protein expression, and immune receptor sequences, and multimodal profiling has helped elucidate cellular states and developmental programs, tumor heterogeneity, and tissue-specific regulatory programs at greater depth than bulk RNA sequencing. [Nature Reviews Genetics](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-023-00580-2)

Most recently, there have been major advances in spatial transcriptomics that provide a critical missing feature of traditional dissociative scRNA-seq: spatial information. By preserving transcript information in space, spatial approaches are bridging the molecular identities of cells to tissue structure and cell-cell communication. High-throughput sequencing, multi-modality, spatial profiling, and ever-more powerful statistical and machine learning approaches have brought scRNA-seq to a status beyond simple measurement to a fundamental tool for building cellular atlases and understanding disease.

With microfluidic droplets, barcoded gel beads and unique molecular identifiers, Chromium enabled high-throughput and parallel analysis of thousands of individual cells at once, vastly improving the throughput while lowering costs and effort compared with plate-based methods like Smart-seq2. This era of revolution was timely, following the launch of the Human Cell Atlas at the Wellcome Trust in London on 13–14 October 2016, which created the large-scale infrastructure for defining human cells and their states in different tissues. [10x Genomics](https://s28.q4cdn.com/592666581/files/doc_news/2016/10/18/10x-genomics-announces-new-low-cost-single-cell-instrument.pdf) [Human Cell Atlas](https://www.humancellatlas.org/event/human-cell-atlas-launch-meeting/)

The scale and scope of scRNA-seq has since grown. Through advances in droplet chemistry, sequencing and computational pipelines, scRNA-seq studies have scaled to hundreds of thousands to millions of cells, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing has been developed for analyzing frozen and archived tissues and tissues with difficult dissociation into single cells. Other parallel developments have integrated transcriptome information with other modalities, such as chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, protein levels, and immune receptor sequences. These multi-omics methods have improved our understanding of cellular states, developmental processes, tumour heterogeneity and tissue-specific regulatory networks, compared with bulk RNA-seq analysis. [Nature Reviews Genetics](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-023-00580-2)

A key limitation of dissociative scRNA-seq has been alleviated with recent spatial transcriptomics studies. Spatial methods maintain the information on where transcripts are located, bridging the gap between molecular identities of cells and tissue structure and cell–cell interactions. The advances in high-throughput sequencing, multi-omics integration, spatial measurements and increasingly sophisticated statistics and machine-learning approaches have transformed scRNA-seq from a niche measurement technology to a key technology for creating cellular atlases and understanding diseases.
